articles.title: Karl Bushby completes English Channel swim
articles.summary: The adventurer is nearing the end of his 28-year journey home to Hull from Chile.
articles.body:
Adventurer Karl Bushby says he has completed a multi-day swim of the English Channel, stepping foot on UK soil after a 28-year journey.

Bushby, 57, left Chile, South America, on 1 November 1998, following two self-imposed rules - not to use transport to advance and not to return home until the journey is complete.

On Tuesday, he announced that he had swum from France to the UK - the final, major hurdle of his journey back to his childhood home in Hull.

Bushby said: "[It] feels good to have UK soil under my feet after all these years. It hasn't been easy, and that's part of the point; proving I'm more capable than I give myself credit for."

He added: "All of us can accomplish more than we will ever imagine."

Bushby said he swam for 20 hours over three days, making landfall at Shakespeare beach, just south of Dover, at 15:30 BST on Monday.

HM Coastguard said it "liaised with French authorities and maritime sector partners to ensure safety protocols were met".

Bushby's team said he was welcomed on the beach by a small gathering of friends and family, including his father, Keith Bushby, a former SAS soldier, and acclaimed filmmaker Werner Herzog, who is directing a feature-length documentary about the journey titled Walk of Life.

For many years, the French have only tolerated cross channel swims departing from the UK - not from France.

However, Bushby's team said permission had been sought from both French and UK authorities, and said they chose not to publicise exactly when it would take place "for safety and security reasons".

To date, Bushby has covered more than 30,000 miles (48,000km), including 29 countries.

He walked the length of South America, crossed the treacherous Darien Gap and continued north to Alaska.

From there he crossed the Bering Strait on foot, swimming where necessary.

Bushby then traversed Siberia and the rest of Asia before swimming across the Caspian Sea, which took 31 days to complete.

He crossed into Europe last year and arrived at the English Channel last month.

The journey has been dogged by problems, with visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash which cost him sponsors, Covid-19 and geopolitics having all stopped him in his tracks.

In June, Channel Tunnel bosses vetoed his request for access to a service tunnel , which he said left him with no other option than to swim.

In September, when the BBC met Bushby in Belgium, he said how he felt it was "definitely time to call it a day", adding: "I don't want to keep this going for much longer."

He said he had always been fascinated with nature and horizons, which fuelled his thirst for adventure.

It is expected he will reach Hull by early November.

articles.title: Metal detectorist finds second Bronze Age hoard seven miles from first near Peebles
articles.summary: Dubbed the Blyth Hoard, the artefacts dating from between 1150BC to 850BC were found seven miles from the Peebles Hoard.
articles.body:
A metal detectorist has revealed his "quite extraordinary" discovery of a second Bronze Age hoard in the Scottish Borders.

Mariusz Stepien found his latest haul of 3,000-year-old treasure in 2022 at a spot seven miles from where he discovered the Peebles Hoard in 2020.

Dubbed the Blyth Hoard, the artefacts date from the Late Bronze Age between 1150BC to 850BC.

They feature two bronze axe-heads, and clay moulds potentially used to make some of the unique bronze fittings in the nearby Peebles Hoard - which was saved for the nation in 2024.

The hoard also includes a complete copper ingot, which is said to be the first of its kind found in Scotland.

Excavation by archaeologists further revealed an ancient stone cairn.

The Blyth Hoard has now been brought to the National Museums Collection Centre in Edinburgh for conservation and analysis.

Experts hope that analysis of the ingot might point towards the geographical source of the metals used in the making of the bronze objects in both hoards.

Dr Matthew Knight, curator of prehistory, Bronze Age collections at NMS, said: "This is one of those classic archaeological finds that initially doesn't look like much, but is actually really incredible and has many stories to tell.

"It's really rare for mould materials to survive at all, so it's a special find in its own right, but the proximity and relationship to the Peebles Hoard makes it all the more extraordinary."

Mariusz Stepien said he was looking forward to seeing what further research could reveal about both hoards - and about the people behind them.

"When I first discovered the Blyth Hoard, I was excited to have found more Bronze Age material in an area that I already knew was archaeologically significant," he said.

"At that stage, I had no idea just how important the discovery might turn out to be.

"Having previously discovered the Peebles Hoard, it is quite extraordinary to think that two discoveries I made so close to one another could be connected."

The Peebles Hoard includes a complete horse harness discovered by Stepien.

Archaeologists later excavated a sword still in its scabbard, decorated straps, buckles, rings, ornaments and chariot wheel axle caps.

Under Scots law, archaeological finds discovered in Scotland must be reported to the Treasure Trove Unit , based at NMS, where they are recorded and assessed.

Significant finds may be claimed on behalf of the Crown by the King's and Lord Treasurer's Remembrancer and allocated to museums through the Treasure Trove system, where they can be preserved and enjoyed for public benefit.

articles.title: O que um elefante-marinho de 3 toneladas faz no Rio? Entenda a visita | G1
articles.standfirst: Animal de cerca de 5 metros foi visto em São Conrado, Niterói e Copacabana. Especialistas explicam por que a espécie, incomum no litoral carioca, pode ter chegado até aqui e alertam: apesar da aparência tranquila, é preciso manter distância.
articles.summary: Elefante-marinho no Rio de Janeiro: animal de 3 toneladas visto em Copacabana e Niterói está apenas descansando, mas especialistas alertam para manter distância por segurança.
articles.body:
Um visitante de quase 3 toneladas e cerca de 5 metros de comprimento tem chamado a atenção de quem passa pelas praias do Rio de Janeiro e de Niterói nos últimos dias. O elefante-marinho, uma espécie que não costuma frequentar as águas cariocas , já foi visto em São Conrado, na Zona Sul do Rio, em Icaraí, em Niterói, e, nesta terça-feira, em Copacabana.

A presença do animal na região há vários dias desperta uma série de perguntas : de onde ele veio? Está perdido? Por que passa tanto tempo deitado na areia? Quanto tempo pode ficar no Rio? E há algum risco em chegar perto dele?

Segundo biólogos, aparições como essa são incomuns, mas podem acontecer. Uma das hipóteses é que o animal tenha chegado à costa do Rio acompanhando correntes marítimas mais frias e buscando alimento.

Da esquerda para a direita: o elefante-marinho em Copacabana, em Icaraí, em Niterói; e em São Conrado — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo e Fabrício Pioyani/ AgNews

Não necessariamente. Elefantes-marinhos são capazes de percorrer grandes distâncias pelo oceano em busca de alimento. Durante esses deslocamentos, um indivíduo pode acabar aparecendo muito longe das regiões onde a espécie é encontrada com maior frequência.

O biólogo Pedro Fróes explica que esse não é um animal comum nos mares cariocas e que a passagem pelo Rio pode estar relacionada justamente a esse deslocamento em busca de comida.

A hipótese, portanto, não significa necessariamente que o elefante-marinho tenha perdido a capacidade de voltar. O deslocamento pelo litoral pode fazer parte de uma movimentação temporária.

Elefante-marinho na orla de Copacabana, na Zona Sul do Rio, na manhã desta terça-feira (6) — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

Por que ele fica tanto tempo deitado na praia?

A cena pode preocupar quem encontra um animal desse tamanho imóvel na areia, mas o simples fato de um elefante-marinho permanecer deitado na praia não significa que ele esteja doente .

A saída da água é importante para o descanso desses animais. Por isso, aproximar-se para tentar fazê-lo voltar ao mar pode ter justamente o efeito contrário ao desejado: interromper um período de repouso.

Em Copacabana, o elefante-marinho passou boa parte do tempo praticamente no mesmo lugar. Deitou de barriga para baixo, virou de barriga para cima, enterrou parte do rosto na areia, se coçou e chegou a bocejar.

Em determinado momento, quando parecia disposto a sair da água novamente, encontrou uma aglomeração de pessoas e voltou para o mar.

Elefante-marinho na Praia de Copacabana, na Zona Sul do Rio — Foto: Josué Luz/ TV Globo

É o mesmo animal visto em diferentes praias?

Os biólogos acreditam que sim. Segundo os especialistas que acompanham o caso, o elefante-marinho visto em Copacabana é provavelmente o mesmo que apareceu anteriormente na Praia de Icaraí, em Niterói, e, antes disso, em São Conrado, na sexta-feira (2).

A sequência ajuda a mostrar que o animal está se deslocando pela costa da Região Metropolitana.

Não é possível saber exatamente. A permanência depende do comportamento do próprio animal e das condições que encontrar durante o deslocamento. Ele pode continuar aparecendo em diferentes praias antes de seguir viagem.

Por isso, uma nova aparição não significa necessariamente que o elefante-marinho esteja com dificuldade para deixar a região.

Banhistas observam elefante-marinho na Praia de Copacabana — Foto: Josué Luz/ TV Globo

Elefante-marinho faz aparição discreta em Icaraí, na orla de Niterói, na Região Metropolitana do Rio — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

A aparência preguiçosa engana. Apesar de passar horas aparentemente indiferente à movimentação ao redor, o elefante-marinho é um animal selvagem, grande e territorial. Especialistas alertam que ele possui dentes afiados e pode reagir caso se sinta ameaçado ou encurralado .

O tamanho também impressiona. O animal observado no Rio tem cerca de 5 metros e pesa quase 3 toneladas.

Por isso, a orientação é não tocar, alimentar ou tentar conduzir o elefante-marinho de volta para a água.

O que fazer se encontrar o elefante-marinho?

A principal recomendação é simples: observar de longe .

É importante evitar aglomerações ao redor do animal, não bloquear seu caminho entre a areia e o mar e manter animais domésticos afastados.

Fotos e vídeos podem ser feitos, desde que a aproximação não altere o comportamento do elefante-marinho.

A distância também ajuda o animal a fazer exatamente aquilo que provavelmente procura quando sai da água: descansar.

articles.standfirst: Alessandro Lucas Póvoa, de 40 anos, está preso e responde por pelo menos três crimes. Segundo o Ministério Público, ele praticou atos libidinosos em sala contra vítimas entre 12 e 17 anos. Defesa dele informou que ainda está se inteirando do caso.
articles.summary: Alessandro Lucas Póvoa, de 40 anos, está preso e responde por pelo menos três crimes. Segundo o Ministério Público, ele praticou atos libidinosos em sala contra as vítimas.
articles.body:
Professor vira réu por crimes sexuais no Paraná — Foto: Redes sociais

O professor Alessandro Lucas Póvoa, de 40 anos, virou réu por cometer crimes sexuais contra cinco alunas dentro de um colégio estadual de Cafeara , no Norte do Paraná.

A Justiça aceitou na última sexta-feira (2) a denúncia do Ministério Público do Paraná (MP-PR), que acusa o professor dos crimes de tentativa de estupro de vulnerável, importunação sexual e assédio sexual. As vítimas tinham idades entre 12 e 17 anos.

Os casos aconteceram este ano, dentro de sala de aula. As denúncias foram feitas em setembro deste ano e o professor está preso desde o dia 25. Procurado pelo g1 , o advogado Anderson Costa, que atua na defesa de Alessandro Lucas Póvoa, informou que "ainda está se inteirando do caso".

A denúncia do MP afirma que o suspeito praticou diferentes atos libidinosos , como toques e comentários indevidos, que causaram constrangimento às vítimas. O caso está sob sigilo, por envolver crianças e adolescentes.

O g1 apurou que as investigações sobre a conduta do concluíram que ele solicitava números de telefone de estudantes com o pretexto de oferecer aulas particulares. Os investigadores também descobriram que Alessandro tirava fotos das vítimas sem consentimento e se recusava a apagá-las.

O professor foi contratado por um Processo Seletivo Simplificado (PSS) da Secretaria da Educação do Paraná (Seed). Após a denúncia do Ministério Público, ele foi suspenso da função. Em nota, a Seed informou que adotou os encaminhamentos institucionais e medidas administrativas cabíveis. Confira a nota completa abaixo.

Além do pedido de condenação, o MP também pede na denúncia o pagamento de valor mínimo de R$ 5 mil em indenização a cada vítima.

"A Secretaria de Estado da Educação do Paraná (Seed-PR) informa que acompanha o caso envolvendo a prisão de um professor contratado pela rede estadual de ensino no município de Cafeara e aguarda a conclusão dos procedimentos conduzidos pelas autoridades competentes.

A Seed-PR esclarece que foram adotados todos os encaminhamentos institucionais cabíveis e ressalta que adotará as medidas administrativas cabíveis no âmbito de sua competência, reafirmando seu compromisso com a proteção de crianças e adolescentes.

Informações relacionadas à investigação e aos desdobramentos do caso devem ser solicitadas aos órgãos responsáveis pela apuração e condução do procedimento, no âmbito de suas respectivas competências".

articles.summary: A previsão do tempo em Divinópolis indica chuvas isoladas e trovoadas com máximas de 33°C e alerta de tempestade emitido pelo Inmet até sexta-feira.
articles.body:
clima de chuva em Divinópolis e região — Foto: Anna Lucia/ g1 centro oeste

Divinópolis está em alerta de tempestade e deve registrar tempo nublado, temperaturas elevadas e possibilidade de chuvas isoladas entre quarta-feira (7) e sexta-feira (9), segundo o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet). A umidade relativa do ar pode variar de 30% a 90% no período.

A quarta-feira (7) será de muitas nuvens, com pancadas de chuva acompanhadas de trovoadas. A temperatura mínima será de 19 °C , e a máxima pode chegar a 32 °C . A umidade relativa do ar varia entre 40% e 90%.

Na quinta-feira (8), Divinópolis terá muitas nuvens e possibilidade de chuva isolada ao longo do dia. A temperatura mínima prevista é de 20 °C , enquanto a máxima pode alcançar 33 °C . A umidade relativa do ar deve variar entre 30% e 80%.

Na sexta-feira (9), a previsão aponta muitas nuvens e possibilidade de chuva isolada . Os termômetros devem marcar mínima de 19 °C e máxima de 31 °C . A umidade relativa do ar pode variar entre 40% e 80%.

articles.title: Novos viadutos e túneis em Fortaleza: obras começam em 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Intervenções serão realizadas em pontos estratégicos da cidade e buscam melhorar mobilidade, segundo a Prefeitura. Licitações estão previstas para novembro e dezembro de 2026.
articles.summary: Intervenções serão realizadas em pontos estratégicos da cidade e buscam melhorar mobilidade; licitações estão previstas para novembro e dezembro de 2026.
articles.body:
Cruzamento entre avenidas Aguanambi e Domingos Olímpio, em Fortaleza — Foto: Helene Santos/SVM

A Prefeitura de Fortaleza vai iniciar, em 2027, a construção de seis novos viadutos e túneis na cidade , nos bairros Parangaba, Itaperi, José Bonifácio, Dionísio Torres e no Conjunto Ceará - na divisa com Caucaia.

O pacote de obras foi anunciado pelo prefeito de Fortaleza, Evandro Leitão (PT). Segundo o gestor, as obras irão melhorar a mobilidade urbana na capital, com mais fluidez ao trânsito de importantes avenidas em vários bairros da Cidade.

Ainda de acordo com o prefeito, milhares de fortalezenses serão beneficiados com a iniciativa, principalmente aqueles que se deslocam por transporte público, tendo em vista que as intervenções serão em importantes corredores de ônibus.

Todo o pacote deve custar cerca de R$ 275 milhões - sendo R$ 70 milhões destinados a desapropriações e indenizações. A previsão de conclusão das obras é até o final da atual gestão, em 2028.

Uma das intervenções envolve uma demanda histórica para conectar Fortaleza e Caucaia, entre os bairros Conjunto Ceará e Jurema.

Os editais de licitação já foram publicados pela Secretaria Municipal das Licitações (Selifor), com todas as sessões marcadas para novembro e dezembro de 2026. Os recursos para as obras são garantidos pelo Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina e Caribe (CAF) e pelo Tesouro Municipal.

articles.title: Envolvimento em sequestro leva ex-chefe da inteligência alemã à prisão | G1
articles.standfirst: August Hanning era suspeito de participar no sequestro de duas crianças. Crime foi encomendado pela mãe delas, que é a herdeira de uma famosa cadeia alemã de restaurantes.
articles.summary: August Hanning era suspeito de participar no sequestro de duas crianças. Crime foi encomendado pela mãe delas, que é a herdeira de uma famosa cadeia alemã de restaurantes.
articles.body:
A prisão do ex-presidente do Serviço Federal de Inteligência da Alemanha (BND) August Hanning, nesta terça-feira (6), sob suspeita de espionagem e traição, ocorreu por acaso, após descobertas feitas durante investigações de um outro crime: a suposta participação dele em um sequestro de crianças, segundo relatos publicados na imprensa alemã.

A Procuradoria-Geral da Alemanha, em Karlsruhe, anunciou nesta terça as prisões de Hanning e de seu antigo chefe de gabinete, Manfred D., que teria fornecido a ele informações altamente sigilosas durante vários anos.

De acordo com informações das emissoras WDR e NDR e do jornal Süddeutsche Zeitung, as acusações não estão relacionadas à Rússia. A Procuradoria-Geral não quis dizer para qual serviço de inteligência estrangeiro ou para qual país Hanning teria trabalhado.

Suposto envolvimento em sequestro de crianças

August Hanning, ex-chefe da espionagem da Alemanha — Foto: Michael Kappeler/dpa via AP

Hanning vinha sendo investigado no âmbito de um inquérito separado sobre o sequestro dos filhos da empresária de Hamburgo Christina Block, em janeiro de 2024. A disputa envolve a guarda das crianças com o ex-marido da milionária, que já durava vários anos.

A Promotoria de Hamburgo acusa Christina, herdeira de uma famosa cadeia de restaurantes na Alemanha, de ter encomendado o sequestro dos dois filhos mais novos no final de 2023, que foram retirados do ex-marido na Dinamarca.

Segundo investigadores, Hanning estaria envolvido em uma tentativa anterior de sequestro das crianças, acusação que ele nega.

A família Block é bastante conhecida em Hamburgo, principalmente pela popular rede nacional de restaurantes, a Block House. A disputa judicial pela guarda dos filhos atraiu grande atenção no país, com ampla cobertura dos tabloides alemães sobre o caso.

Segundo informações da WDR, NDR e do Süddeutsche Zeitung, ao analisar o material apreendido com Hanning no ano passado, agentes do Departamento Estadual de Investigação Criminal (LKA) teriam encontrado um dispositivo de armazenamento de dados contendo informações altamente sensíveis, o que levou a Procuradoria-Geral a pedir sua prisão.

August Hanning em 30 de novembro de 2006 — Foto: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

Segundo as investigações, o ex-chefe do BND tinha acesso a documentos ultrassecretos que, em hipótese alguma, ele deveria possuir.

Tratava-se, em grande parte, de informes para as reuniões semanais de inteligência na sede do governo federal, a Chancelaria Federal em Berlim, onde os chefes das agências de segurança trocam informações.

As apurações indicam que os documentos incluíam relatórios extremamente sensíveis, como sobre o programa nuclear iraniano ou o Exército russo. Fontes da área de segurança afirmaram que o material também continha informações provenientes de serviços de inteligência parceiros de outros países.

Entre os serviços de inteligência, o vazamento desse tipo de material é considerado como uma catástrofe absoluta. Agências parceiras poderiam perder a confiança no BND e deixar de compartilhar informações essenciais com o órgão.

O período de serviço de Hanning no BND terminou em novembro de 2005. Ao todo, cerca de 2 mil documentos teriam sido repassados por D. a Hanning, que é acusado de cumplicidade no caso.

articles.title: Rússia ataca a Ucrânia com drones e mísseis; Zelensky diz que 11 pessoas morreram | G1
articles.standfirst: A ofensiva foi realizada com 130 drones, 48 ​​mísseis de cruzeiro e mísseis balísticos, informou a Força Aérea Ucraniana. Unidades de defesa aérea abateram 161 alvos.
articles.summary: A ofensiva foi realizada com 130 drones, 48 ​​mísseis de cruzeiro e mísseis balísticos, informou a Força Aérea Ucraniana. Unidades de defesa aérea abateram 161 alvos.
articles.body:
Fogo e fumaça se elevam na cidade durante um ataque russo com mísseis e drones, em meio ao ataque da Rússia à Ucrânia, em Kiev , Ucrânia — Foto: REUTERS/Vladyslav Sodel

A Rússia lançou uma série de drones e mísseis contra a Ucrânia nesta quarta-feira (7), matando pelo menos 11 pessoas e danificando prédios residenciais, instalações industriais e infraestrutura, segundo o presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelensky.

Mais cedo, as autoridades ucranianas haviam informado que duas pessoas morreram na capital Kiev, quatro na cidade de Pryluki, no norte do país, e duas na região central de Poltava.

"A Ucrânia foi atingida novamente por mísseis russos durante a noite", disse Dmytro Lubinets, comissário parlamentar ucraniano para os direitos humanos, no aplicativo Telegram.

"Mais uma noite sem dormir, mais um ato de terror, depois do qual as pessoas ainda têm que planejar seu dia de trabalho apesar de tudo", acrescentou.

A Rússia lançou 130 drones, 48 ​​mísseis de cruzeiro e também mísseis balísticos para atacar a Ucrânia, informou a Força Aérea Ucraniana. Unidades de defesa aérea abateram 161 alvos, segundo comunicado divulgado no Telegram.

Kiev e Poltava, na região central da Ucrânia, a região sudeste de Dnipropetrovsk e Kharkiv, no nordeste, foram os principais alvos dos ataques russos, informou a Força Aérea Ucraniana.

O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia afirmou que suas forças realizaram um "ataque maciço" contra instalações do complexo militar-industrial em Kiev e outras regiões da Ucrânia, utilizando armamento de alta precisão lançado por terra, mar e ar, além de drones.

Segundo o comunicado, os alvos incluíam locais onde a empresa de defesa ucraniana Fire Point fabrica e armazena seus mísseis de cruzeiro Flamingo e drones de médio e longo alcance em Kiev, bem como regiões de Kiev, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava e Kharkiv.

Na semana passada, o presidente Volodymyr Zelenskiy afirmou que a Ucrânia havia disparado em combate seu primeiro míssil balístico de fabricação nacional, produzido pela Fire Point.

Em entrevista à Reuters na semana passada, Zelensky disse esperar que a empresa tenha um míssil FP-9 de longo alcance pronto até o outono, o qual, segundo a empresa, será capaz de atingir Moscou .

Bombeiros trabalham enquanto moradores caminham perto do local onde garagens particulares foram atingidas por um ataque de míssil russo, em meio ao ataque da Rússia à Ucrânia, em Kiev , Ucrânia — Foto: REUTERS/Valentyn Ogirenko

Em Pryluki, na região norte de Chernihiv, um míssil russo atingiu um prédio residencial de cinco andares, informaram as autoridades regionais. Pelo menos quatro pessoas morreram no local e outras 20 ficaram feridas, enquanto mais moradores podem estar soterrados sob os escombros, disseram as autoridades locais.

Imagens de vídeo mostraram equipes de resgate retirando pessoas debaixo dos destroços.

Muitos moradores de Kiev buscaram abrigo nas estações de metrô subterrâneas da cidade, à medida que autoridades ucranianas e a inteligência militar divulgavam alertas sobre os iminentes ataques.

Diversas explosões estrondosas ecoaram pela capital durante a noite, disseram testemunhas à Reuters.

"O metrô é melhor, porque moramos no 9º andar de um prédio alto, e é realmente assustador estar no 9º andar e mísseis estarem voando na sua direção", disse Lesia, uma moradora de Kiev de 49 anos, à Reuters.

Autoridades ucranianas afirmaram que mísseis balísticos russos, além dos drones, também atingiram Kyiv.

Durante meses, a Ucrânia sofreu com uma grave falta de defesas aéreas, o que levou Zelensky e outros funcionários a pedirem repetidamente ajuda e mais suprimentos.

Ataques aéreos noturnos na cidade de Dnipro, no sudeste do país, danificaram uma instalação industrial, infraestrutura de transporte em Zaporizhzhia e prédios residenciais em Kremenchuk, disseram autoridades regionais no aplicativo de mensagens Telegram.

articles.standfirst: Programação reúne nove opções em Belém e municípios da região metropolitana, com visitas a ilhas, fábricas e espaços de produção a partir desta quarta-feira, 7
articles.summary: A Rota da Bioeconomia no Círio 2026 oferece nove roteiros com experiências amazônicas, incluindo visitas a fábricas de chocolate e cachaça em Belém.
articles.body:
Rotas turísticas ofertam destinos urbanos e também ribeirinhos, como imersão na área de seringal e praia de água doce — Foto: Divulgação

Quem estiver em Belém durante o Círio de Nazaré de 2026 poderá conhecer outros caminhos da região entre uma programação e outra da maior festa religiosa do Pará. A partir desta quarta-feira (7), nove experiências da Rota da Bioeconomia levam moradores e turistas para conhecer desde a produção de chocolate e sorvetes até a extração da borracha, o uso do cumaru e bebidas feitas com ingredientes amazônicos.

São nove roteiros para todos os gostos. Os passeios ocorrem em Belém, Ananindeua, Santa Bárbara do Pará e nas ilhas do Combu e de Cotijuba. Há opções de uma hora, que podem entrar no roteiro de quem tem pouco tempo na cidade, e imersões que ocupam praticamente um dia inteiro.

Na Ilha do Combu, por exemplo, o visitante pode conhecer de perto o cacau e a produção de chocolate artesanal. Em Cotijuba, o percurso passa por um seringal e acompanha a extração do látex e sua transformação em biomateriais e peças de design.

Entre os rotas, dá para conhecer o cultivo do jambu, que é matéria-prima da cachaça de jambu do Meu Garoto — Foto: Divulgação

Para quem prefere ficar na área urbana de Belém, há experiências em torno da cachaça de jambu, dos sorvetes feitos com sabores amazônicos, do cumaru e da destilação de bebidas com botânicos da região.

A programação faz parte da Rota da Bioeconomia, iniciativa da Associação dos Negócios de Sociobioeconomia da Amazônia (ASSOBIO), criada no contexto da COP30 para aproximar visitantes de negócios, produtos e cadeias produtivas da região.

Agora, a proposta é manter as experiências como opção de turismo para além da conferência climática.

“Queremos que quem chega a Belém para o Círio possa conhecer a Amazônia também pelas mãos de quem produz aqui. A experiência muda quando você encontra as pessoas, conhece a origem de um ingrediente, entra em um espaço produtivo e entende o caminho que existe até aquele chocolate, aquela bebida ou uma peça feita com borracha nativa”, afirma Tainah Fagundes, coordenadora da Rota da Bioeconomia pela ASSOBIO.

A Rota da Bioeconomia foi estruturada inicialmente com 11 experiências na Grande Belém e surgiu como uma estratégia para aproximar visitantes de negócios e cadeias produtivas ligados à sociobioeconomia amazônica.

Durante o ciclo da COP30, as experiências e atividades associadas à iniciativa registraram 1.019 participações diretas. Segundo dados do projeto, mais de R$ 300 mil foram movimentados em experiências, comercialização de produtos e ações vinculadas à programação no período.

A iniciativa é realizada pela ASSOBIO com apoio do Governo do Pará, por meio da Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Clima e Sustentabilidade (Semas), no âmbito do Programa Floresta em Pé. A operação comercial da programação do Círio é feita em parceria com a Vida Caboca Turismo.

Historiador Michael Pinho em passeio com turistas na Estação das Docas, em Belém — Foto: Divulgação

Na Ilha do Combu, a experiência passa pelo cacau, chocolate artesanal, frutas nativas e pela história de um empreendimento ribeirinho.

As visitas ocorrem todos os dias, de 7 a 31 de outubro, em diferentes horários.

O roteiro entra nos bastidores da produção de uma sorveteria paraense e apresenta a relação dos produtos com frutas e sabores amazônicos.

As visitas ocorrem nos dias 7, 14, 21 e 28 de outubro.

O cumaru é o protagonista desta experiência, que apresenta a semente, seus usos na gastronomia e na cosmética e as etapas de beneficiamento.

O passeio ocorre no campus da Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA), nos dias 7, 14 e 21 de outubro.

A sensação característica provocada pelo jambu também faz parte de uma das experiências. O roteiro apresenta a cachaçaria Meu Garoto e sabores regionais em uma atividade no centro de Belém.

As visitas estão marcadas para 8, 9, 12, 13 e 14 de outubro.

A experiência apresenta botânicos amazônicos usados na produção de bebidas e processos de destilação e experimentação.

Há programação nos dias 9 e 10 de outubro.

Em Santa Bárbara do Pará, a experiência propõe uma vivência sensorial em torno do cacau amazônico, com música e meditação.

O roteiro ocorre nos dias 12, 15 e 17 de outubro.

O roteiro começa no Terminal de Icoaraci e segue para Cotijuba, onde o visitante conhece a seringueira, acompanha a extração do látex e entra em contato com a produção de biomateriais e design.

O passeio ocorre nos dias 14, 15, 17 e 19 de outubro e ocupa praticamente o dia inteiro.

🚶 ASSOBIO — Entre tradição e inovação na Rota da Bioeconomia

O roteiro começa no Ver-o-Peso e passa por pontos que ajudam a contar diferentes momentos da relação de Belém com produtos e saberes amazônicos.

O caminho inclui Estação das Docas, Porto Futuro II e espaços do Parque de Bioeconomia, além de uma experiência de degustação no Tekoá. O percurso termina na Vitrine da Bioeconomia, espaço que reúne produtos de empreendimentos amazônicos.

As saídas ocorrem nos dias 13, 14, 19, 21, 26 e 28 de outubro.

Em Ananindeua, o visitante conhece o cacau e acompanha a produção artesanal de chocolate a partir da experiência de uma família empreendedora paraense.

As visitas ocorrem nos dias 17, 18, 24 e 31 de outubro e 1º de novembro.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Badenoch promises tax cuts' and 'Asos hacker havoc'
articles.summary: The Tories' financial plans and a hack at online shopping outlet Asos lead Wednesday's papers.
articles.body:
The Daily Mail is one of a number of papers looking ahead to Kemi Badenoch's speech at the Conservative Party conference. It says on its front page that her plan to "slash" employers' national insurance contributions will get young people "back to work". The Sun hails the plan with the headline, " the lady's Neet for turning" , saying it could be a "lifeline" for those not in education or training. The Times reports that Badenoch will also pledge to cut the rate of inheritance tax . It says her tax cuts would be funded by £30bn of welfare reductions.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a £1bn package of support for poorer households to help them with their energy bills, according to the Guardian. Sources tell the paper no final decisions on the Budget have been made, and officials are also considering more radical changes to how much energy companies can charge customers.

The i reports that the budget for schools in England will be squeezed, after Education Secretary Lucy Powell announced a pay rise for teachers would be fully funded, without consulting the Treasury. The paper quotes teaching unions as saying there will now be "no new money" for schools. The Treasury and the Department for Education both deny the claims.

The Daily Mirror carries a warning from Cancer Research that the NHS will miss its cancer diagnosis and treatment targets by over three years. The health service's current goals are for 2029, but the charity says it won't meet them until 2032, unless things improve. The Department of Health said it had already made significant changes but there was a lot more to do.

Andrew Mountbatten Windsor's legal action against Thames Valley Police centres on allegations officers took his personal items , claims the Daily Telegraph. The paper says the former prince believes private and confidential material was removed during searches of his home in February, as part of an investigation into allegations of misconduct in public office. Mountbatten-Windsor denies wrongdoing.

The Times has picked up that his old Bentley, which once bore a personalised Duke of York number plate , is up for sale. The green Flying Spur, which has only 7,000 miles on the clock, could be yours for £125,000.

articles.title: As the US government wants to change the clock 'forever', researchers in Canada warn; call it a 'time bomb' for ...
articles.summary: A renewed political drive in the United States to end seasonal clock adjustments by locking in year-round Daylight Saving Time is facing resistance from
articles.body: A renewed political drive in the United States to end seasonal clock adjustments by locking in year-round Daylight Saving Time is facing resistance from both Capitol Hill and the medical community. While President Donald Trump has put heavy pressure on lawmakers to pass the measure -- calling for extra evening sunshine for recreation and business -- a growing body of scientific evidence warns that the policy could trigger chronic public health damage. Incidentally, some members of Congress in the US have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it got stalled in the House.The debate reignited this week with the publication of a research review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. As several Canadian jurisdictions weigh ending their own clock changes, researchers examined the physiological fallout of permanent daylight saving time compared to permanent standard time. Their findings endorse permanent standard time as the healthier option, cautioning that extended evening light paired with darker winter mornings runs counter to the fundamental biology of the human body. For those unaware, Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time.Why researchers are against 'changing' the clockAccording to the authors of the research report, the human circadian rhythm runs on a natural cycle of roughly 24.2 hours and relies critically on natural morning sunlight to reset and synchronize essential bodily functions. While later daylight hours may accommodate evening commutes and outdoor leisure, delayed sunrise suppresses natural wakefulness. Conversely, lingering evening light delays the internal clock, disrupting sleep quality, mood, and daily productivity.The consequences of late-shifted sunlight are already visible along the geographic borders of current time zones, where sunrise and sunset can vary by over an hour within a single zone. The Canadian review cited evidence showing that Americans living on the western edges of time zones -- where the sun sets later -- lose roughly an hour of sleep each week compared to those on the eastern side. The researchers concluded that while abolishing biannual clock adjustments eliminates a few weeks of acute disruption each year, the consequences of permanent daylight saving time would be chronic. Their recommendation aligns with broad consensus across international chronobiology and sleep medicine organizations, including a 2024 guidance from British sleep specialists advocating a permanent lock on Greenwich Mean Time.Permanent daylight bill: Where it stands right nowCalled the Sunshine Protection Act, it passed in the House in July this year, but faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.Despite these warnings, legislative momentum in Washington remains contentious. While the U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time, the bill has stalled in the Senate. The impasse even prompted President Trump to escalate public pressure, going so far as to post the personal mobile phone number of Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas on social media.Defending his stance, Cotton noted that previous attempts to lock the clock to summer hours collapsed once citizens faced the reality of dark winter mornings. Historical records support the pushback: the United States previously adopted permanent daylight saving time during World War II and again during the 1973 energy crisis, with Congress repealing the 1970s initiative after less than a year amid intense public outcry over morning darkness. Similar nationwide trials in Russia and Chile were also later reversed due to public dissatisfaction, safety concerns, and body-clock disruption.Canadian researchers further note that a permanent shift by the United States would place severe economic pressure on Canada to follow suit, regardless of medical advice.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
articles.summary: Campaigners say ruling sets a precedent requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.
articles.body:
Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minimised to the greatest extent practicable”.

Environmental campaigners called Wednesday’s court decision the first ruling on climate change. They said it set a “binding national precedent” requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.

In the ruling, three of the High Court’s five judges found that the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in New South Wales must be halted. Planning authorities, they said, were obliged to consider granting consent only with conditions ensuring that all greenhouse gas emissions were minimised, and had not done so in this case.

The case was brought by retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, who had fought for years to halt the planned mine expansion in Australia’s rural coal-digging heartland.

“Today the High Court has said what we have always known,” Wales said in a statement. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.”

The mine’s operator, Mach Energy, had sought to extend the life of the open-cut mine in the Hunter Valley by more than 20 years, to 2048, and to nearly double its annual output. Mach is owned by Droxford International, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s Salim Group.

Mach argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental effects felt near the mine.

The company’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission. But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely.

“Today, the highest court in the country agreed that those decisions have to account for the damage they cause,” said Lonergan. “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.”

Australia is one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, ranking among the top sellers of both coal and liquefied natural gas.

Anita O’Hart, a lawyer for Wales and Lonergan’s community group, said the “historic” ruling was expected to affect how future fossil fuel projects are handled.

“The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project’s emissions through to real, local climate harm,” she said.

“This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.”

Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision.

“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

images.caption: Wendy Wales, president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (right) and Tony Lonergan (centre) in, Sydney, Australia, on 7 October 2026 [Courtesy of Climate Media Centre]

articles.title: Pornhub returns to Australia but only for adults with Apple devices
articles.summary: The world's most popular porn site went dark in March in Australia due to age verification laws.
articles.body:
Pornhub has returned to Australia, eight months after it went dark due to age verification laws, but only adults with Apple devices will be able to access the site.

On Wednesday, parent company Aylo said it was restoring access for "eligible adult users in Australia" who have "confirmed their age through Apple's Australian age-verification process".

The world's biggest porn site left the Australian market in March, saying new laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 would not protect children and "instead creates harms relating to data privacy" and exposure to content on non-compliant platforms.

Apple recently introduced new age checks in Australia, following a rollout in the UK.

In March, Australia introduced stricter laws requiring users to prove they were over 18 in order to access adult content such as porn, R-rated video games and sexually explicit AI chatbots.

The country's online safety regulator said the changes would protect children from harmful content and platforms would be fined for breaches.

Critics said there would be issues with data privacy and users finding ways to trick age-verification technologies such as facial recognition, digital IDs and credit card details.

Aylo said it was returning to Australia as Apple has "set a benchmark" by setting default child safety features on all devices unless owners confirmed they are adults.

This, in effect, makes "every phone or tablet kid-safe as a starting point," it said.

"For years, Aylo has advocated for device-based age verification as the most effective and privacy-protecting approach to help prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content online," said Aylo's vice-president of brand and community Alex Kekesi.

Australians with Apple devices that have been "age-verified" will be "served a standard adult users experience", she said.

Apple users can prove they are over 18 using a credit card, their passport, a driver's license or a government-issued ID.

Kekesi added that having devices with child safety features as a default meant adults don't have to "surrender unnecessary personal information to multiple apps and websites".

It also limits the usefulness of virtual private networks (VPNs) to circumvent age-verification technologies, she said.

VPNs are commonly used to trick a site into thinking a user is logging on from another country, giving the user access to the site.

articles.title: Battle of ideas looming in British politics, Badenoch to say
articles.summary: The Tory leader has been seeking to reframe the way the public views her party, which has yet to recover in the polls since the last election.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch will say there is a "battle of ideas" looming in British politics when she delivers a speech on the final day of her party's annual conference on Wednesday.

Badenoch is expected to tell delegates in Birmingham that the differences between her party and the Labour government go "to the very core of what kind of country we want to be".

This week the Tory leader has been seeking to re-frame the way the public views her party, which has yet to recover in the polls since the last election.

The party has already pledged £10bn for a UK air defence system , and proposed cuts to the rate of employer National Insurance contributions for those aged 21 to 24.

There is also speculation that Badenoch could propose changes to inheritance tax. According to the Times , Badenoch is due to announce a cut to the 40% rate of the tax.

That rate applies to a person's estate worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren. Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24 inheritance tax was paid on 4.72% of estates and raised around £7bn for the government.

Asked if Badenoch would announce a new policy on the tax, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart told BBC Breakfast: "Kemi has said she'd like to abolish inheritance tax but it's very important we can afford any announcement we can make.

"That is why she has asked Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, to see what is possible - when that work is finished we will make an announcement."

The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

During her main conference speech, Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than those of her party, will pitch the fight against Labour at the next general election as "a battle for the soul of this nation".

She will say there is now a clear distinction between the Conservatives and Labour under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

According to extracts released in advance, Badenoch will say Burnham's government wants to "wind back the clock to failed ideas of the past".

"They believe economic growth is created by politicians. They think government knows best.

"They think that your income, your pension and your savings are theirs to take and then hand out as they see fit."

Badenoch will add that Labour will "claim what they are doing is compassionate", but the result will be higher taxes and a poorer country caught in a "doom loop".

By contrast, Conservatives believe "what people earn belongs to them, not government", Badenoch will say - adding that growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government".

Earlier this week, Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Chancellor John Healey said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies

Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back'

Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system

The Conservatives have laid out a number of plans during its autumn conference for if it enters government at the next general election.

On Tuesday, Badenoch said she was proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) contributions on earnings for those aged 21 to 24 from 15% to 7.5%.

Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training, and the government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities.

The Conservatives said the policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.

The move would cost £2.3bn, according to party estimates, with a plan on how to fund it to be published on Wednesday.

Earlier this week, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights.

He said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

The Tory leader will argue her party is "a renewed Conservative Party fighting again for the belief that what people earn belongs to them, not government".

In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason on Tuesday, she said "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved".

articles.title: U.S. military restricts troops from leaving base in Japan after Marine is arrested in a killing
articles.summary: The Marine’s arrest has renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the island of Okinawa and the rise in military-related crime.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. military in Okinawa, Japan, is pausing all operations for two days, restricting the ability of troops to leave their base and ordering training after a Marine was arrested on suspicion of killing a local woman. Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said in a letter posted on social media Tuesday that episodes like these “demand we pause for reflection” and that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.” The arrest of the Marine has renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island and the rise in military-related crime. The killing could also complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to strengthen the Japanese military on Okinawa and to work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China in the region. “We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region. Accordingly, we will take time to think hard about discipline, standards and our alliance responsibilities.” The 48-hour pause will last from Wednesday through Friday. Service members will receive training on standards, discipline and “our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community.” Restricting the ability of troops to leave military bases and interact with the local community is a common response by military leaders to major crimes. Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island’s capital city, Naha, early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media. Ballard is from Ohio, the Marine Corps said. Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone. Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported. “I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times. He was referring to the U.S. military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases. People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, but some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China. Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with about 30,000 being active-duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces. There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military. The number of such criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to police. After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime.

images.caption: This picture taken on August 23, 2022 shows a general view of the US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma from Kakazutakadai Park in Ginowan, Okinawa prefecture. For decades, residents of Japan's Okinawa have strongly opposed the US military bases that dot the region, but a subtle shift is underway, driven by Chinese sabre-rattling and economic challenges. articles.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
articles.summary: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.
articles.body:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.

"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.

While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.

Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."

That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?

Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.

There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.

When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.

"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.

But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.

Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.

It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.

"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."

Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".

"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."

And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".

"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.

Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.

For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.

It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.

"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"

Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.

"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."

While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.

Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.

According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.

"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."

Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.

The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.

It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.

"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."

He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.

"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.

"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.

That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.

He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.

However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.

"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.

If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.

"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.

articles.title: Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas attacks grapple with how to rebuild
articles.summary: Three years on from the attack on Nir Oz, in which 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage, some survivors have returned to live there.
articles.body:
Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.

"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.

By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.

The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."

As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.

Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.

The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.

Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.

"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.

"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."

An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.

Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.

Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.

As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.

The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."

The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.

The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.

On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.

Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.

Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.

"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."

"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."

While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.

Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.

Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.

They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.

"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.

However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.

"Terrorists penetrated 97% of the households and burned down almost 50%," says Emi Palmor, director of the rebuilding project. "Now it's the only place in Israel that has to be completely demolished and completely replanned."

She says that it is a difficult balance to redesign the kibbutz so that it feels like home but does not cause new trauma to those who return.

"It's a huge debate – a very painful debate," Emi says. "Some people say, 'If I come back here, I want the entire area to look serene. I don't have to be reminded because I remember every day the people I lost.' Other people say, 'There is such denial – if we will take down the last houses, who will ever believe?'"

About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage after an estimated 6,000 Palestinians streamed across the Gaza border during the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN.

Despite the US-brokered ceasefire deal which brought the last hostages home a year ago, violence has continued, including near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced and much of the territory is in ruins. US President Donald Trump's peace plan is at an impasse.

For Israelis, there are outstanding questions over accountability for the failure of Israel's security forces to have prevented the 7 October attacks. People from Nir Oz favour a comprehensive state commission of inquiry and still have major security concerns.

Survivors, including the Aharons, suffer from post-traumatic stress. Dalit recalls how her eldest son, Uri, turned nine on 7 October 2023 - when they spent the day hiding in their bomb shelter. "He told me, 'Mum, I don't want to die on my birthday,'" she says. "You know people don't understand that we still live this horrible day."

This anniversary of the attacks is the first with no hostages remaining in Gaza. "It's a very big relief," Dalit says. Achi sees that now is the time to focus on personal healing.

"Until the hostages came back, it was the only thing on our mind," he says. "Now you have the time to concentrate on yourself, on what you lost, what you need. Now it's our recovery or some kind of recovery as much as we can."
