articles.title: Sick leave approved, but SBI declared his job ‘voluntarily vacated’: Why Patna HC quashed its Rule 40(3) action
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can a bank treat an employee as having voluntarily resigned after a long absence from work if his medical leave was earlier approved and he had
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can a bank treat an employee as having voluntarily resigned after a long absence from work if his medical leave was earlier approved and he had submitted medical records? The Patna high court recently examined this question while hearing a challenge by a State Bank of India (SBI) employee who was treated as having voluntarily vacated his job after remaining absent from duty.The high court found that the bank had not properly examined the employee’s medical grounds or given him a fair opportunity to explain his absence before taking the drastic step of treating him as having left the service. It quashed the bank’s orders and directed SBI to reinstate the employee with continuity of service, but without salary or allowances for the period he did not actually work.What was the dispute between the SBI employee and the bank?According to the court order, the employee had joined SBI in 1989 and was later promoted as assistant manager and then deputy manager. The dispute arose after he was transferred from the bank’s Digha branch in Patna to the Muzaffarpur Zone in June 2019 and was required to report at the Regional Business Office in Bettiah.He reported at the Muzaffarpur Zone on June 25, 2019, and worked there till June 28. He then applied for medical leave after being diagnosed with jaundice and claimed that he was advised complete rest for 45 days. His leave from July 1 to July 31 was approved through the bank’s HRMS system.The employee later said he developed severe pain in his leg and remained under treatment. He was admitted to a private clinic on October 17 and claimed that he eventually reported at Bettiah after being declared medically fit in December.However, SBI later treated his absence as unauthorised. The bank said the leave had been approved by an authority that was not competent to sanction it and that the employee was required to report at Bettiah.What action did SBI take against the employee?SBI communicated on October 22, 2019, declining the leave and treating his absence as unauthorised from June 29.It then issued a notice on November 6 asking him to report for duty and explain his absence within 30 days. The notice warned that failure to do so would mean he had voluntarily vacated his employment.A second notice dated December 13 declared that he had voluntarily vacated his service with effect from December 7 and directed him to pay an amount equivalent to three months’ salary.The employee challenged the action before the bank’s appellate authority, but his appeal was rejected in June 2020. He then approached the Patna high court.What did SBI argue?The bank argued that the employee had sought a particular posting after his transfer but, after that request was not accepted, he took medical leave instead of joining at Bettiah.SBI also argued that the sick leave had been approved by the Digha branch manager even though the employee had already been relieved from that branch. According to the bank, the approval was an administrative mistake and could not give him a right to remain absent.The bank further said the employee had remained absent for more than 90 consecutive days and that it had followed the procedure under Rule 40(3) of the SBI Officers’ Service Rules, 1992.What does Rule 40(3) of the SBI service rules say?Rule 40(3) deals with prolonged absence from duty or overstaying leave. Where the conditions under the rule are met, SBI can issue a notice asking an officer to report for duty within 30 days.If the officer does not report within that period, the appointing authority can treat the employee as having voluntarily vacated the employment.The high court, however, said Rule 40(3) could be invoked only after the bank first determined whether the absence was actually unauthorised or amounted to overstaying leave."The scheme of Rule 40, therefore, requires the authority to first determine whether the absence of the officer is, in fact, unauthorized or amounts to overstaying of leave within the meaning of Rule 40(2). It is only upon the requisite conditions being satisfied that the consequence contemplated under Rule 40(3) can be invoked against the concerned officer," the high court said.What did the Patna high court find?Justice Harish Kumar examined the employee’s medical records, the earlier approval of his leave through the HRMS portal and the procedure followed by SBI before treating him as having voluntarily vacated his service.The court noted that the employee had submitted medical prescriptions and reports and that the bank had not specifically found those documents to be forged or fabricated. It also noted that he had received full salary for the period for which his sick leave had been approved.The court said that even if the Digha branch manager was not competent to approve the leave, the application should have been forwarded to the competent authority."Even if, for the sake of argument and for the present, the contention of the Bank is accepted that the leave was sanctioned by an authority who was not competent to grant such leave at the relevant point of time... the least that was expected of the respondent-authorities was to forward the petitioner’s application to the competent authority for proper consideration of his request for sick leave," the court said.It further held that the earlier approval could not be used to simply reject the employee’s medical claim without examining whether his medical reasons were genuine."The factum of such approval could not, by itself, constitute a valid ground for completely discarding the petitioner’s claim for sick leave without examining the genuineness and bona fides of the medical grounds on which such leave was sought," the court said.The high court also distinguished between absence from work and wilful absence."Mere absence from duty without an application for leave or prior permission may constitute unauthorized absence, but it does not invariably follow that such absence is wilful," it said.The court found that SBI had not given convincing reasons for rejecting the medical documents. If the bank had doubts about their genuineness, it could have verified them or referred the employee for examination by a medical board.It also found that the appellate authority failed to properly consider the earlier HRMS approval and payment of salary. The employee had not been given a fair and meaningful opportunity to explain his alleged unauthorised absence before the drastic consequence was imposed."The impugned action, therefore, also suffers from violation of the principles of natural justice," the court said.The court concluded that SBI’s action did not meet the requirements of fairness and reasonableness under Article 14 of the Constitution.What did the Patna high court order?The high court quashed SBI’s notices dated November 6 and December 13, 2019, which treated the employee as having voluntarily vacated his service. It also set aside the appellate authority’s order dated June 24, 2020.The court directed SBI to:Reinstate the employee with continuity of service.Count the period of absence for continuity of service and other consequential service benefits, subject to the applicable rules.Not pay salary or allowances for the period during which the employee did not actually work.The writ petition was allowed and both sides were directed to bear their own costs.

articles.title: Where has £450m of investment for the Border region gone?
articles.summary: At the halfway stage most of the projects in England are delayed and only three have been completed.
articles.body:
It began as a promise to boost the economic fortunes of the five council areas either side of the England-Scotland border.

After years of negotiations, the Borderlands Growth Deal was finally signed in 2021.

Hailed as an "ambitious approach to cross-border working", nearly half a billion pounds of investment was promised from the UK and Scottish governments over a decade.

But at the halfway point, only three projects in England are fully complete, and the deal has been criticised for delays and bureaucratic setbacks.

One million people live in the Borderlands region, in the five local authorities of Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, Northumberland, Dumfries and Galloway, and the Scottish Borders.

The deal brought the five authorities together to invest public money on projects aimed at growing the economy, boosting tourism, and regenerating local areas.

Over 10 years, the Scottish and Westminster governments agreed to spend £452m on projects which would create jobs, improve transport and digital connectivity, and increase jobs in tourism and green energy.

But those who hoped the funding would unlock major infrastructure schemes like dualling the A1 between Northumberland and Scotland, dualling the A69 between Carlisle and Newcastle, or extending the Borders Railway to Carlisle, will have been disappointed.

Just one of those infrastructure schemes would have swallowed the entire budget.

Councillor Glen Sanderson, the Conservative leader of Northumberland County Council, said "people sat down and said how can we invest in the little towns and little villages in the Borderlands? How can we actually all work together, with the Scottish government and the Westminster government, to find enough money to do things that would not normally happen?"

Smaller developments in market towns, for example, involve community interaction and open calls for ideas. Larger projects involve consultation between local councils and communities.

All of the ideas then go through business evaluations before funding is agreed.

Patricia Bell, a Liberal Democrat councillor on Westmorland and Furness council, said: "It really is a place-based project. It's not just about investing in one project - it's saying, how can we use that investment in a number of different ways to support the town's future?"

The first project completed in Cumbria was the renovation of Penrith playhouse.

"It's just made us feel like we're on the map a little bit now," said Natasha Binder, from the Penrith Players.

"The Borderlands said, you are a charity group that is deserving of this money and so we've been able to say to people, 'look at us. Look how much good we can do and how much good we are already doing.'"

Penrith has also got new street signs in the town, and funding has been promised to upgrade Castle Park.

Scott Jackson, chairman of the planning committee at Penrith Town Council, said: "Council finances can be tight, but when the opportunity comes along to fix one of the things that people notice could be done better in the town - I think it's excellent."

But the two biggest projects in Cumbria are far from complete.

The Borderlands deal is funding most of a £40m upgrade of Carlisle railway station.

It should have been finished in summer 2025 but work has stalled, and costs have risen.

"We've no idea what's going on," said Cumberland Liberal Democrat councillor Brian Wernham.

"We were promised that the relocation of the car park to the other side of the station with a new entrance would have opened last year. Nothing's going on on this site," he said.

Cumberland Council's latest update on the project, from April 2026, stated that the station gateway plans had been approved.

The Citadels redevelopment project is also well behind schedule.

The University of Cumbria campus is due to be relocating to the site, using £50m of Borderlands funding, but an agreement over the land ownership has only just been reached.

In September, Cumberland council said work was continuing on the proposals.

Despite the delays, supporters of the Borderlands Growth Deal said residents should not lose faith.

"There are quite a lot of bureaucratic hoops to jump through. And it's taking a long time," councillor Patricia Bell of Westmorland and Furness Council said.

She said the holdups were easy for her to understand as a councillor, but "very difficult for the public to understand".

"Nevertheless, thank goodness we have Borderlands, because we wouldn't have the investment otherwise," she said.

Work has recently started on the Roxy theatre in Ulverston, and Egremont and Dalton-in-Furness are also waiting for regeneration projects through the Borderlands Place Programme .

Northumberland has arguably enjoyed more success than Cumbria from the Borderlands growth deal.

Two out of three major projects part-funded by the Borderlands deal are already complete and open, including the Lilidorei playpark at the Alnwick Garden, and the Ad Gefrin whisky distillery in Wooler.

Alnwick is getting £2m of funding through the Place Programme for regeneration projects, including reopening Northumberland Hall as the new home of the Bailiffgate museum.

Chris Ferguson, trustee of the Bailiffgate museum, said the Georgian building has had "so many stop starts in its history".

"We were just really fortunate when we got support from the Borderlands to be able to move in here and do something new with it for the people of Alnwick and the town," he said.

Alnwick bus station is also about to be refurbished with better lighting and seating, and an improved entrance for buses.

The famous cobbles in the town are also due to be restored.

The town council said work on all three projects was due to start "very soon".

But the third and final major project in Northumberland backed by Borderlands funding has stalled.

Berwick's redeveloped Maltings Theatre should have been ready to open by now but work has yet to begin, after lengthy arguments over the building's design.

The cost has also soared from £17m to £36m.

Work is finally due to start in November, subject to Northumberland County Council agreeing to pay £7.5m towards it, but critics of the deal have not been impressed.

Councillor Scott Dickinson, the leader of the Labour group on Northumberland County Council, said the delays have been "frustrating" and "communities in places like Newbiggin and Prudhoe are still waiting for things that have been promised that simply haven't materialised".

"Over a million pounds worth of administrative costs gets spent every year, and people aren't seeing the value of projects because nothing's happening in some places," he said.

Supporters of the Borderlands Growth Deal insist it has brought success to England's most northern counties.

Sanderson, a Borderlands Board member, accepts the delays have been frustrating.

But he said there were complexities involved because you are working with the Westminster and Scottish governments.

"There are various groups of civil servants in between and it can look very slow," Sanderson said.

But he said when the decisions are made "the results are there and wonderful results they are".

Sanderson said he believed the deal was "making a great deal of difference" and "there will be more to enjoy".

articles.title: Survivors ask why Sheffield rapist was able to flee to Pakistan
articles.summary: Amar Ilyas left the UK while on bail for sexual offences, and never returned for his trial.
articles.body:
Three women who were sexually abused by a serial rapist have said they feel "betrayed" and "frustrated" after their attacker fled to Pakistan while on bail.

Amar Ilyas, 41, was convicted of 20 sexual offences against five girls in Sheffield and was sentenced, in his absence, to a minimum of 27 years in prison.

One of his victims told the BBC she had assumed his passport would automatically be surrendered after he was charged and said she was "so disappointed in the law."

The government said "decisions on bail restrictions are a mattter for the independent judiciary", while the National Crime Agency (NCA) said it was "making every effort to ensure Ilyas is brought before the court".

A woman who was sexually abused by Amar Ilyas when she was 13 said she had been "cheated" because she felt unable to go out and leave her home, yet her abuser had been able to leave the country.

"There is no justice is there really? He didn't take accountability. He's not getting any consequences for his actions," she said.

"We were told that he got to keep his passport because of his human rights but he wasn't humane towards other people.

"He didn't show any empathy so it was a really big insult when his human rights and feelings were taken into consideration."

Amar Ilyas was arrested in 2020 and charged in 2023, as part of the NCA's Operation Stovewood, investigating sexual abuse in South Yorkshire.

Sheffield Crown Court heard he had carried out the offences against girls as young as 12 in the Meersbrook and Sharrow areas of Sheffield between 2004 and 2007.

The BBC understands he was allowed to keep his passport after appearing in court and had previously travelled abroad while on court bail, but had returned to the UK.

He went to Pakistan in July 2025 and did not return for his trial in September of that year, despite being ordered to fly back to the UK by the judge.

His younger brothers are both currently in prison for sexual offences against one victim. Kamar Ilyas, 40, was jailed for 10 years and Kamran Ilyas, 39, was sentenced to three years.

Another woman said she had learning difficulties and was in a very vulnerable, dark place when she was abused by Amar Ilyas as a teenager.

"Why, when he's committed these offences against us girls, was he allowed to keep his passport? That's my question. Where is the justice?" she asked.

"I hope they find him and I hang on to that hope every day, maybe it will be tomorrow, it might be next year but we have to hang on to hope."

A third woman, who was raped by Amar Ilyas as a teenager, said she did not have much hope that he would return to the UK to serve his sentence.

"I just know he's in Pakistan and they're doing what they can, but I've been told it's very difficult with Pakistan with extradition," she said.

"Shame on him but shame on the law too, they allowed that to happen."

The women, who have the right to lifelong anonymity, said they had taken the decision to speak to the BBC to call for changes to prevent sex offenders absconding during court proceedings.

"Going forwards, I think they need to put into place that they remove the passports," one said.

"We live in a world, unfortunately, where these things are carrying on happening.

"There are survivors coming forward but survivors might not want to come forward after hearing something like this."

Judge Peter Hampton, who did not oversee the bail condition applications at earlier hearings, but sentenced all three brothers in June, described Amar Ilyas as having "taken the coward's route and fled".

In his sentencing remarks, he urged law enforcement to locate him and use "all means" to execute the arrest warrant that remains outstanding.

It is understood that when Amar Ilyas's defence team applied for bail, which the prosecution had the opportunity to contest, no request for his passport to be forfeited was made.

Phillip Marshall, head of Operation Stovewood for the NCA, said officers were carrying out proactive enquiries.

He said: "Amar Ilyas tormented and brutally sexually abused vulnerable young girls and women 20 years ago, and he has callously compounded their decades of suffering by not returning to the UK for his trial or sentencing."

Marshall added: "Operation Stovewood's meticulous investigation ensured that despite the passage of time, complexity of the case and Ilyas's absence, his crimes against the women were heard, believed and proven in court.

"We are just as determined to ensure that Ilyas serves his prison sentence."

Lucy Duckworth from the Survivors Trust described the case as "absolutely appalling" and said it demonstrated the need for specialist courts and training in sexual violence response for staff in the criminal justice service.

"It doesn't make sense the way we are treating this crime if we're saying, 'you're such a risk to society' and yet we're giving bail and we're allowing them the freedom to potentially commit that crime again or to evade justice by leaving the country," she said.

"I think it is widely accepted that the criminal justice system is currently failing victims and survivors and that needs to change.

"I hope that cases like this can highlight the massive gaps and make sure that we all work together and work with the government to get the changes in place needed."

In response to the story, a government spokesperson said: "These were horrible crimes, and our thoughts remain with the victims.

"More broadly we're determined to protect vulnerable girls and bring those responsible to justice. That is why we're cracking down on vile abusers as part of our mission to halve violence against women and girls in a decade."

articles.title: Blind and visually impaired people fear smart glasses backlash
articles.summary: Smart glasses are banned in some venues but disabled wearers describe them as game-changing.
articles.body:
Sitting at his desk with some post in front of him, Darren Paskell puts on his glasses and says: "Hey Meta, read aloud all the text you can see on the letter."

Within seconds a female voice reads the words on the page. For the past 18 months, Darren, who is visually impaired, has used smart glasses for tasks including sorting through post and reading labels.

"They're really good for identifying different jars in the kitchen," said Darren. "I'm in my 40s now and this is the first time that I've been in a position to wear something, talk to something and, with a single command, get the information that I'm looking for. This technology is absolutely life-changing for me."

Darren, who works for the charity Guide Dogs, wears the glasses at home, but would like to use them more in public.

He said: "It would be great to have an idea what's happening on the street while I'm walking down it, or where are the queues if I'm looking to buy something."

However, a number of venues have restricted the use of the glasses, which have a tiny camera embedded in the frames.

The glasses are banned in courtrooms and some schools, as well as some pubs, restaurants, cinemas and theatres .

This followed concerns about their use. It can be difficult to tell when the camera is on, and some women have reported being secretly recorded by the devices and then harassed .

The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active.

Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica reported that it sold seven million pairs last year.

Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021.

Darren, who travels from his High Wycombe home to the office in Euston for work, said he was worried about how the backlash towards the technology could affect him.

"It is concerning for me when I'm not allowed to use them," he said.

"That is essentially a little bit like an organisation saying: 'As a blind person you're not welcome coming into this place'," he said.

Sight loss charities agree. Khadija Raza, the Royal National Institute of Blind People's policy lead on accessibility, said the unintended consequence of organisations banning the devices could be that blind and partially sighted people "feel less safe and ultimately excluded from activities that others take for granted".

Khadija said the institute urged venues and service providers to take an "inclusive, proportionate approach" to the technology that protects privacy but also allows blind and partially sighted people to use smart glasses.

Rachel Taylor, technology programme lead at the charity Guide Dogs, said she expected the number of people with sight loss who use smart glasses to increase.

"Guide Dogs calls on businesses and venues to consider the use of AI wearables as a reasonable adjustment, recognising the vital role these devices can offer," she said.

But the stigma around the devices seems to be growing.

They have been nicknamed " pervert glasses " and were mocked in a series of unauthorised adverts and signs in London.

Stickers that were designed to look similar to Transport for London (TfL) safety notices were placed on the London Underground by activist group Everyone Hates Elon. The group also organised billboards that dubbed the devices "pervert technology".

A spokesperson for the group said: "As a woman in London, you feel really unsafe. The last thing we need is more things that help abusers to do things without our consent.

"That's why these glasses are really scary and we wanted to tell people about the risks of them and make them culturally unacceptable."

They said the group wanted to shame people wearing the devices, adding: "We don't want to be filmed all the time. I think you're seeing a global pushback against a loss of privacy."

TfL said unauthorised adverts that appeared on its network were removed as soon as they were identified.

Liz Hunter said she was so appalled by the glasses that she helped launch a petition and database called Stop Smart Glasses, which invites people to contact their local retailers and ask them not to sell the technology.

Liz said: "The government has not caught up, law hasn't caught up with this.

"What we're seeing is big tech racing ahead, again, of regulation. Now we're in this awful mess where consent is supposedly an LED light in a pair of glasses. That is not consent."

Liz added: "They're being used for blackmail, for sextortion. They are an absolute infringement of our human rights. The general public is infinitely more at risk because of these devices."

Filming people in public is generally legal, but it can still breach harassment or stalking laws, and filming people in places where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy may be unlawful.

A spokesperson for the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said: "The government has no current plans to introduce specific legislation on the use of smart glasses for filming in public spaces because there are already criminal offences in place to deal with harmful conduct."

The Meta glasses revolution - is it okay to film people in public?

Campaigners argue smart glasses have legitimate uses for people with visual impairments, but should not be widely used in public.

A spokesperson for Everyone Hates Elon said: "Meta have some of the best technologists and brains in the world. So let's see them focus on helping disabled people, rather than trying to profit so much from our imagery, our voices and our data".

Meta said its glasses provided valuable accessibility benefits for blind and other disabled users and could help users navigate their surroundings, access information and carry out everyday tasks more independently.

It has previously said that, as with any recording device, people using smart glasses should not engage in "harmful activities like harassment, infringing privacy rights, or capturing sensitive information".

articles.title: Worcester landlord urges government to cut tax for hospitality
articles.summary: A pub landlord forced to close down says more venues face similar closures without more tax cuts.
articles.body:
A publican has revealed his anguish at having to close down, saying he has been "crippled" by rising costs and a decline in customer drinking habits.

Jon Dean, who ran The Alma Tavern in Worcester for the last seven years before closing its doors this week, has urged the government to consider new tax cuts for hospitality venues or face more pubs going under.

He said: "We employed 14 or 15 people here but we've had to let everyone go. It's a bitter pill to swallow."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said pubs "were already benefitting from a 20% cut in business rates", with Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously calling it "the first step" to help the industry .

Dean, who also lives above the pub, is having to find a new home after opting to hand the business back to the brewery, Star Pubs.

"We've been trying to keep it going but there's no light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

"Hospitality has taken a battering. We've had the utility crisis, the cost of living crisis [and] now the war in Iran.

"All of that has had an impact on prices, but when you add in employer's national insurance contributions, rocketing minimum wage, rocketing VAT, business rates, all of that pressure has crippled us."

Dean told the BBC that customers were not spending as much, something he put down to the cost of living pressures.

"People used to come in four or five times a week and they'd have four or five pints, but those days are gone," he said.

"Now we'd maybe see them once or twice a week and they might only have a drink or two - people just haven't got the money.

"I've tried everything to keep the pub going, but it's like flogging a dead horse."

Explaining the financial pressures, he said: "A place like this turns over maybe £800,000 a year, but once you've paid out your taxes, your energy bills, your wages, it's pretty much all gone.

"Taxation and the cost of everything is just far too high."

In July, the government cut business rates for pubs.

But last month, more than 800 businesses, including top UK chefs, wrote an open letter to the PM , saying there would be more pub and restaurant closures unless VAT was reduced.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of the trade body UKHospitality, said the tax burden for the sector had "grown disproportionately" in recent years.

"We have already seen promising signs from the new government in its approach to hospitality - I hope this [forthcoming] Budget will see further backing for the entire hospitality sector," he added.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The chancellor has prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues, saving thousands of [pubs] over £1,000 a year.

"This is on top of providing a tax break on poured pints and capping corporation tax."

A spokesperson for Star Pubs said: "While Star Pubs owns The Alma Tavern, it is leased to an independent operator who runs it as their own business and has taken the decision to close the pub."

articles.title: Mayor of London race 2028: Conservatives seek party's nomination
articles.summary: The Tory party has closed applications to be their candidate for mayor and there are four hopefuls.
articles.body:
"We need to treat London seriously" - the words of a leading Conservative MP as his party considers its next candidate to be mayor of the capital.

The party has just closed applications for the role and there are four runners who have openly declared.

In 26 years, the Tories have only had one mayor in the capital, Boris Johnson, who won two elections and served from 2008 to 2016.

The party has lost three elections since then to Sadiq Khan, now Lord Khan of Tooting.

Gareth Bacon MP, shadow minister for London, told a meeting at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham this week that his party had treated the mayoralty like a "paper candidacy" in the past two elections - meaning that they hadn't taken it seriously enough.

Bacon said that the party had "cut Susan Hall adrift", a reference to their candidate in the last mayoral election in 2024, when Lord Khan won that historic third term as mayor.

Bacon went on to describe Lord Khan as "toxic and divisive".

The election for mayor of London will be held in May 2028.

That is more than 18 months away, but the race is well under way.

Reform UK selected their candidate, Leila Cunningham, in January.

Sarah Olney, MP for Richmond Park, and Rob Blackie, who ran in 2024, are both candidates for the Lib Dem nomination.

This time round, with speculation about whether the current mayor will stand for a fourth term, the Conservatives sniff a chance.

On the back of local elections in May 2026 when the party won back traditional strongholds like Westminster and Wandsworth from Labour, they feel the mood may be changing.

However, winning the mayoralty may be too big a task. Much of it will depend on who they choose as their candidate.

As the putative front runner, Braintree MP and former home secretary and foreign secretary James Cleverly has been working the conference circuit very hard.

Once a London Assembly member, and former head of the London Fire Authority, he is seen by many Tories as the 'shoe-in' candidate.

But he will come with baggage - he is a Brexiteer and when he was head of London's Fire Authority oversaw a big cuts programme.

He told me: "I hope to be a real champion for London, not just an administrator. I would make sure people are safe on the street and can really make a life for themselves and their families and can afford to live in London."

Cleverly said party political affiliations "are less important than someone with a real plan to make London a city we can be proud of again".

He added: "I hope to get the candidacy and then be a real champion for London, not just an administrator but a real champion and it's the city I love and that's why I want to put myself forward."

Festus Akinbusoye is a relative newcomer to London politics, though not to the city.

He emigrated from Nigeria with his parents and sister at age 13 in 1991 and lived in Canning Town in east London.

Akinbusoye was the Bedfordshire police and crime commissioner from 2021 to 2024 and was elected to Westminster City Council in May.

He told me: "We do not have to accept that this is the best we can get.

"I believe that we don't have to accept that just because we're a global city, London has got to be so unaffordable to build a life in.

"I want to be the most pro-policing, pro-house building, pro-business, pro-family, pro-growth mayor London has ever had.

"We can make that happen because London works when Londoners work".

Andrew Boff is the current chair of the London Assembly.

Privately, Conservatives joke that it wouldn't be a mayoral selection without him in it. He's been an assembly member since 2008.

They also know he thinks very deeply about the capital's issues, particularly housing.

He told me: "I've got a very ambitious programme of not telling people how much I love London - because I'm hoping all the candidates love London - but specifically what I'm going to do.

"One of the things we've got to do is help the family housing crisis, so I will make sure we get more money for building those important family-sized homes.

"We need more encouragement for young people to do self-building in housing, so I'll be making land available for young people to build their own homes without having to pay for the cost of the land."

Boff added: "I'll get rid of the outward extension of the Ulez."

Public affairs professional Alex Challoner told me he came to London from the West Country when he was 21 and has called the city his home for 35 years.

He said: "I think as a party, we have a choice between winning and losing for a fourth consecutive time.

"If we're serious about winning we have to have some of the boldest policies that will appeal to Londoners.

"I'm proposing a crackdown on fair dodgers at the Tube barriers by introducing British Transport Police, as well as training up Transport for London staff to stop people breaking through the barriers."

He told me his plan, called Fare Watch, would use a "simple reporting tool in the TfL Go app and online" where passengers will be able to report persistent fare dodging.

Challoner also pledged to introduce "a London Plan that you can read in an afternoon" as well as VAT cut "for gyms and London breweries".

The hopefuls in the race to be the Conservative mayoral candidate will have to wait until November to find out if they've made the final shortlist.

It is believed that London party members will then be offered a choice of two candidates.

I'm told the final two are likely to be announced on 20 November.

The original proposed date had been Friday the 13th, until it was pointed out that that may not be the most auspicious date to unveil candidates.

articles.title: How the drought hit UK farms: Half the harvest, double the bills
articles.summary: Farmers gathered much less wheat in 2026 and dairy farmers' costs rose.
articles.body:
The hottest summer on record, the longest drought, the worst harvest. West Country farmers are counting the cost of a "terrible summer", as one put it.

The wheat harvest on Charles Day's family farm in Gloucestershire was cut in half. "It's just soul-destroying," he says.

Dairy farmers had to rip open silage clamps stored up for the winter to feed the cattle as the grass failed. Sarah Godwin calculates it cost her family's Wiltshire farm "over £100,000". She says "it's shocking".

I spent the summer watching farmers install showers for cows , watch their cauliflowers burn to a crisp in the heat, and search for apples in cider orchards reduced to a tenth of their normal crop.

So now the harvest is home, just how bad was it?

Buy a loaf of bread and there's a good chance it started in the fields of Charles Day's family farm in north Gloucestershire.

"I love harvest," the fourth generation farmer tells me. "It's a whole year's work coming to fruition."

But 2026 was brutal. The crops were looking "fantastic" in April, he told me. Then in June, the rain stopped and "the sun just stole our yield".

Throughout the crucial weeks of June and July, there was no rain at all. Wheat grains shrivelled instead of fattening, and the yield plummeted.

Official figures estimate the total UK cereal harvest was the lowest on record , wheat down about three million tonnes, or 11% according to the Agricultural and Horticultural Development Board (AHDB).

Anthony Hopkins, AHDB director of cereals and oilseeds, says: "At a time of high input costs, arable farmers in the worst-affected areas are really feeling the financial pressure right now."

But in the South West, it was much hotter and the impact far worse.

When the combines went out on Charles Day's family farm, they gathered a harvest "about 50% down, sometimes more".

Across the South West, Tom Collins, who speaks for the NFU in Wiltshire, says most cereal farmers had seen harvests down "at least 30%". Spring barley and beans were more than 50% down, he adds, particularly badly hit by the drought.

"Most farmers will give this harvest 3 out of 10", he adds. "They're pretty depressed."

Put some butter on your bread, or cheese, and that is probably from the West Country's other farmers - dairy producers.

But unlike the wheat harvest, the amount of milk produced this summer barely fell. Total production is down just 4.5% , according to the ADHB.

"That's because we have to feed our cows, and milk them, whatever the weather," explains Sarah Godwin.

Her family raise dairy cows west of Chippenham, selling their milk to a major supermarket.

The Cotswolds was badly hit by the drought, leaving grazing pastures brown and without any nutrition for the cows. So like many farmers, the Godwins had to open their sileage planned for the winter and buy in feed to boost their cows diets.

"Altogether it cost us around £100,000," Godwin explains. "We also had a drop in production yields, that's around £20,000.

"On top of that, cows suffered more lameness, lower fertility, more mastitis. They really did not enjoy the heat."

The family spent £15,000 installing new sprinkler systems and huge fans to cool the cattle in their sheds when they sheltered from the heat outside. All vital for animal welfare, but more costs to the business.

Even the normally lush fields of Somerset withered in the heat. Tom Kimber's family have farmed near Charlton Musgrove in south Somerset, in the heart of England's most productive grazing land. They run 250 dairy cows on their own grass, cutting sileage for the winter months.

By September, they would normally have three large clamps of sileage ready for winter. This year, they have only cut two, and had to raid one throughout July and August, to make up for the lack of grass.

But sadly, Tom Kimber is getting used to what was once freak weather.

"This is the fourth drought in eight years now, so you barely financially get over the last one and you're hit with another one. It's becoming far more frequent, these events.

"It's incredibly difficult this constant lurching between one extreme to the other, that's what keeps you awake at night."

Climate scientists are clear that weather like this is the new normal.

"What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal," says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office.

In Gloucestershire, Charles Day's family have a rare asset: a lake. Fed by a local river, it fills through the winter and then can be used in the summer. They grow salad onions, broccoli and other vegetables on fields nearby, all irrigated by the lake water.

The family wants to expand the lake, hold more water, do their bit to turn winter floods into summer irrigation.

"But it's so complicated," Day explains. "The red tape, the planning, the licences, the digging - it will be very expensive. And we just get no help from government."

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced in the summer a package of support measures including grant funding to construct reservoirs and irrigation infrastructure.

Others are trying to farm in a more nature friendly way. Planting mixed grasses which cope better with drought. More trees to provide shade, older varieties of cereals that withstand heat better.

All these cost money, and there are government schemes to support them. But when the latest round of financing opened, it was overwhelmed.

A year's worth of government grants, more than £250m, was handed out in under six hours in an online scramble "reminiscent of Glastonbury ticket sales", as Wiltshire farmer Tom Collins put it.

"It just shows how desperate farmers are," he adds.

"It's so hard to make a living from food people fall over themselves to get these environmental grants, and then they're swallowed up in no time. It's so unfair."

A spokesperson for the Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs says: "In anticipation of high demand, ministers decided to allocate an additional £20m to the fund, on top the £50m announced by the prime minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible."

Farming Minister Stephen Morgan adds that the Sustainable Farming Incentive had been designed to be simpler to apply for and that farmers had "responded in force".

Tom Kimber was one of those who missed out. He went online to apply for an extension of an environmental scheme his farm was already running.

"We plant a mix of different grasses that cope better in the drought," he explains. "But they cost more, so we need the grant."

A glitch in the Defra computer system left him locked out of the website for hours. When he got back in, the money had all gone.

Farming, he says, is not easy at the moment.

"When you're being squeezed from both ends, the milk price is 10p litre below the cost of production, and costs are going up all the time.

"You're just forever hoping for a better day, but hope doesn't keep you in business."

articles.title: Creeslough: Dad to keep promise to daughter 'even in death'
articles.summary: Leona Harper was one of 10 victims of an unexplained explosion at a service station four years ago.
articles.body:
Leona Harper's coat still hangs in the hallway of her family home.

The soil from the pitch of the last game she played is still on her rugby boots.

Four years on from the Creeslough explosion that claimed the 14-year-old schoolgirl's life, along with nine others, her father says their family remains "desperate for answers" about the events of that day.

No official explanation has been given for the cause of the explosion, and no one has been charged in connection with the blast despite a number of arrests.

Gardaí (Irish police) sent a second file to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) in April which is in addition to the primary file it forwarded to prosecutors last September.

A commemoration service will be held on Wednesday in Creeslough for the 10 victims of the explosion.

Leona had travelled to the village for a sleepover.

She had been going to the shop at the service station for ice-cream when the blast occurred.

Hugh Harper said that four years on, the family feels no closer to the truth about what happened to his daughter.

"You are trying to establish answers yourself - but it takes you down a maze of rabbit holes," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme .

"One question leads to another and it just feels like torture and torment.

"We go home every evening to a house that's not the same - we are still trying to adjust to that.

"You never expect something like this to come to your door as a parent and when it does, and it was so sudden, it is very hard."

The Harpers, along with other victims and their families are campaigning for a public inquiry into the Creeslough explosion.

Hugh Harper said he believes a public inquiry is the only path to the full facts.

"We are steadfast on that - a public inquiry is the only tool to compel people to be questioned under oath and get definitive answers.

"Leona went to Creeslough on a Friday afternoon and went into a shop - that's the last we seen or heard of her alive.

"Every day, we grieve for our little girl - we are stuck on the 7th October 2022.

"When I get up in the morning, the first thought I have is about Leona and the questions around her last moments.

"Until we have answers - our grief is frozen in time."

Harper said the family will travel to Creeslough on Wednesday to remember their daughter and the other victims.

"When Leona was born, I was the first to hold her.

"I made her a promise that I would keep her safe and not let anything happen to her and unfortunately, I couldn't keep that promise.

"But even though Leona is not physically here, I feel she is still with me.

"And I will continue with the promise, even in death. I will do my best to protect her name and get to the bottom of exactly what happened in Creeslough that day.

In a statement to BBC News NI, a spokesperson for the Irish Department of Justice said:

"As the fourth anniversary of the Creeslough explosion tragedy approaches Minister [Jim] O'Callaghan's thoughts continue to be with the families, loved ones, survivors and the wider community of Creeslough.

"The focus of the Creeslough investigation remains on ensuring that the investigative processes are allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice so that the full facts can be established."

Gardaí said "the victims, their families and the community are in our thoughts" on the anniversary.

"An Garda Síochána continues to appeal to any person with any information in relation to the fatal explosion – to please come forward and speak to the garda investigation team."

A spokesperson for Ireland's Director of Public Prosecutions said it does not comment on individual cases.

The 10 victims of the explosion included four men, three women, two teenagers and a five-year-old girl - all from the village or surrounding areas.

Those who died were Robert Garwe and his five-year-old daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe; Catherine O'Donnell and her 13-year-old son James Monaghan; Jessica Gallagher; Martin McGill; James O'Flaherty; Martina Martin; Hugh Kelly; and 14-year-old Leona Harper.

articles.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier recently filed a civil lawsuit against Wi-Fi router manufacturer TP-Link.
articles.body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier recently filed a civil lawsuit against Wi-Fi router manufacturer TP-Link. The lawsuit accuses the company of misleading Florida consumers about its products’ security and its ties to China. In the 59-page lawsuit, Uthmeier said that Chinese state-sponsored hackers exploited TP-Link routers sitting in American living rooms. “Many of those models cannot update themselves automatically, and TP-Link has stopped supporting them”. “They also told Floridians they had split from China and that they build U.S. products in Vietnam. That is fiction. Research and manufacturing remain rooted in China. Less than 1% of the parts in that Vietnam plant actually come from Vietnam,” he further added.TP-Link has now responded to the lawsuit, issuing an official statement saying that it is a US company, and not a ‘Chinese’ firm. “TP-Link Systems is a U.S. company that complies with U.S. privacy and data protection laws,” the company said adding “Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseles”.Here’s what TP-Link saidIn a press release, Steve Kovsky, corporate affairs officer for TP-Link Systems Inc. said “The coordinated lawsuits are built on false premises. They do nothing to advance national security while unfairly penalizing an industry-leading U.S. company”.“We stand fully behind the security of our products, the integrity of our company and our people, and our commitment to serving the best interests of our customers in the United States and globally. We look forward to refuting these baseless allegations in court,” Kovsky added.In the release, the company further stated”: “For months, California-based TP-Link Systems has provided state regulators with clear, verifiable documentation demonstrating two fundamental facts: TP-Link Systems devices sold in the U.S. are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, U.S. company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.”“Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseless. TP-Link Systems is a U.S. company that complies with U.S. privacy and data protection laws. We perform comprehensive security testing and rely on trusted third-party security labs for additional scrutiny to ensure our products meet the highest security standards and are recognized as among the most secure on the market. We meet or exceed all industry best practices for monitoring and preventing vulnerabilities and actively support our customers to mitigate any issues that occur as they are identified. We do not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Energy costs: 'Wear more clothes if it's cold', pupils and staff told
articles.summary: The EA suggests cost-saving measures as it warns school gas and electricity bills are set to rise.
articles.body:
Staff and pupils at schools across Northern Ireland have been told to "wear more clothes" if it is cold in order to cut heating bills.

Schools have been told by the Education Authority (EA) to reduce heating and lighting "wherever possible".

The authority has said that school gas and electricity bills are set to rise by about £8m by March 2027.

The EA has written to school heads warning that increasing costs will affect school energy bills.

The impact of the US-Israel war with Iran is one of the factors behind the increase.

The letter from the EA to head teachers said that "recent geopolitical events are expected to have a substantial impact on energy costs across the Education Authority (EA) during the 2026/27 financial year".

It said that total school gas bills were expected to go up by 60% from £10.7m to £17m by March 2027.

Meanwhile, total school electricity bills are expected to rise by 5% from £23.8m to £25.1m by March 2027.

"Given the scale of the anticipated cost increases, we are asking all schools to review their energy usage and identify opportunities to reduce consumption wherever possible," the EA said.

Among the measures the authority has suggested to schools are cutting heating use by an hour a day and switching off classroom lights to use natural daylight instead.

Staff and pupils have also been advised to "wear more clothes" rather than turn the heating thermostat up if it is cold.

But principals have told BBC News NI that it is not straightforward for schools to cut heating costs.

The principal of Tullygally Primary School in Craigavon, Kirsty Logan-Hall, said that the school was "committed to promoting responsible energy consumption and regularly reinforce good practice with staff and pupils".

"However, our ability to achieve significant reductions in energy usage is constrained by the nature of our estate," she said.

"The school operates from an older building which presents inherent energy efficiency challenges.

"In addition, our site is particularly spread out due to the accommodation and operational requirements associated with our specialist provision.

"This necessitates the heating, lighting and ongoing use of multiple areas across the site throughout the school day to ensure appropriate learning environments, accessibility and pupil welfare.

"It is important to recognise that there is limited scope for reducing energy consumption without adversely impacting the quality of provision, staff working conditions or the wellbeing of pupils, including those with additional needs."

Emma Quinn from Rathcoole Primary told BBC Good Morning Ulster that the "lack of maintenance" has an impact on schools, adding that pupils have a right to come into a warm school after being outside.

"Putting this pressure onto us at the minute is ridiculous, when we are eco schools, we are doing all of these, we are turning off lights, but yet this lands in on our doorstep and we're suddenly expected to jump and to fix a problem that is so systemic, it's just not good enough."

Meanwhile, the principal of Holy Evangelists Primary School in Dunmurry, Claire Robinson, said that energy costs were "ferocious".

"We can't play around with the heating," she said.

Parts of the school are relatively new and have underfloor heating.

"Our classrooms can't drop below a certain temperature so we have to keep the heating on," Robinson said.

"We can't just turn the heating off in some areas of the school."

Robinson said that although the school was relatively new it had been given an energy efficiency rating of D due to the costs involved in running the heating system.

articles.title: At least two killed in Kyiv as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia’s Defence Ministry says its forces carried out a ‘massive strike’ on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed in a Russian missile attack on Kyiv as Moscow said it launched a “massive strike” across Ukraine.

Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were killed in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood in a fire caused by the overnight attack.

“Two people were rescued while the fire was being extinguished,” he wrote on Telegram on Wednesday.

“The bodies of two people who had been killed were found.”

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had carried out a “massive strike” on targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions.

The ministry said Russian forces hit port facilities in the Odesa region, as well as sea vessels used in the interests of Ukrainian armed forces.

Kyiv has come under relentless bombardment in recent weeks, with Russian air attacks on energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including the bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro River.

Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.

articles.title: American man claims he ‘cured’ his asthma and allergies by having simple Indian food; gets hilarious replies from netizens
articles.summary: An American man has gone viral after claiming that eating simple Indian food helped him “cure” his asthma and allergies.
articles.body: An American man has gone viral after claiming that eating simple Indian food helped him “cure” his asthma and allergies. What made the video even more amusing for Indian viewers was the food he used to explain his discovery: a packet of aloo bhujia from an Indian brand. Samuel Hillclimber, a Massachusetts-based man who posts on Instagram as @cowboymansam, shared a video praising Indian food and its spices. In the video, he talks about how the ingredients commonly found in Indian food felt medicinal to him and claimed they helped with his asthma and allergies.But while talking about Indian spices, Samuel is seen holding a packet of aloo bhujia from an Indian brand and reading out its ingredients. “Cumin, mango powder, garlic powder, onion powder, lemon powder, turmeric powder, mint leaves,” he says, listing the ingredients one after another. He then praises the food and says that the spices are “extremely medicinal” for his stomach.“I cured my asthma and my allergies by using simple Indian food”In the video, Samuel makes a strong claim about his health and credits Indian food with helping him. “I cured my asthma and my allergies by using simple Indian food, okay? The spices in the Indian food are just extremely medicinal on my stomach. Cumin, mango powder, garlic powder, onion powder, lemon powder, turmeric powder, mint leaves. Come on, dude. It's just amazing on your stomach, and it's gonna cure your asthma and your allergies. Like, you think we didn't have technology to cure asthma before inhalers? We did,” he said.His comments quickly caught the attention of viewers, particularly Indians who found his choice of aloo bhujia unexpected. The video also prompted a wave of humorous reactions in the comments section, with users imagining what might happen if Samuel moved on from aloo bhujia to some of India's other popular foods.“Aloo bhujia was unexpected”One user joked, “Be careful, samosa might unlock your chakras too.” Another wrote, “I don't think highly processed packaged food can cure anything brother.” “Well... Aloo Bhujia was unexpected,” another user commented. An Indian user admitted, “As an Indian, I did not know aloo bhujia cures asthma😂” Another joked, “Imagine if he has Chyawanprash, he will become superman😂” One viewer suggested that Samuel's next discovery should be an iconic Indian dish: “Wait until he discovers Hyderabadi dum biryani.” Some users, however, agreed with part of what Samuel was saying. One person wrote, “I agree most of these spices are medicinal!” And another joked about what could happen after trying another popular Indian snack: “He’ll become super human after one golgappe.”The video has therefore turned into less of a discussion about asthma treatment and more of a light-hearted conversation around Indian spices, snacks and the unexpected things that can go viral online. Samuel's statements about curing asthma and allergies are his personal claims and should not be taken as medical advice or as evidence that aloo bhujia or Indian spices can cure these conditions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
articles.summary: Police in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.
articles.body: HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said. Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others are being investigated for theft, state media said Monday. Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city’s north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night. Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations. The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals. In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam’s dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat. Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims. Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported. The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running. Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners. Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77). In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

articles.title: Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia?
articles.summary: Iran’s oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help.
articles.body:
Countries in Central Asia have begun buying oil from Iran as the Russian fuel supplies they have long depended on run dry amid Ukraine’s mounting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure to degrade Moscow’s war effort.

In August, Tajikistan announced it was receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran as Dushanbe faces uncertainty over its fuel supply from Russia. Tehran also agreed to establish a joint refinery in Kyrgyzstan in August, and supply the country with crude oil.

Moscow has been facing fuel shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries as Russia’s war on its neighbour continues to rage.

Can the Russian fuel crisis give Iran a new oil opening in Central Asia?

Which Central Asian countries have been affected by Russia’s fuel crisis?

Ukraine’s offensive against Russian energy infrastructure has caused panic across Central Asian countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, which are dependent on Moscow for oil and petroleum products.

Tajikistan has traditionally sourced up to 80 percent of its petroleum products from Russia. Kyrgyzstan also relies on petroleum product imports, sourcing more than 90 percent of its petrol from Russia.

“They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which has its headquarters in Berlin, told Al Jazeera in an interview in August.

Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions.

Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova added.

Kazakhstan, meanwhile, boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries. Still, fuel prices in the country have increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10.

Uzbekistan, on the other hand, is less dependent on Russian energy, with domestic production capable of reaching 100,000 tonnes of petroleum products per month, satisfying most of the country’s needs. But due to the increase in oil demand from its regional neighbours, Uzbekistan has also been forced to diversify its imports and has begun striking deals with countries like Georgia and Iraq.

Russia has been facing a severe fuel deficit as Kyiv’s drone strikes – launched in an effort to degrade Moscow’s ability to maintain its ongoing invasion of Ukraine – have knocked out an estimated quarter to half of its total oil refining capacity.

To tackle the problem, Russia has imposed fuel rationing. Sales are often limited to about 20-30 litres (about 5-8 US gallons) per vehicle, and drivers must pump fuel strictly into vehicle tanks. Filling jerry cans is largely prohibited.

Earlier, the government banned petrol and jet fuel exports. Officials are now weighing a ban on diesel exports, too. Authorities have loosened fuel-quality regulations, temporarily allowing lower-grade fuel for the domestic market.

A state of emergency has also been declared in Russian-occupied Crimea , which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014. A Russian-owned oil firm in India, Nayara Energy, has reportedly sold petroleum to Russia.

While Russian President Putin acknowledges the crisis, he appears reluctant to end the war on Ukraine and insists the situation is under control.

“These attacks on our facilities certainly create problems – that is obvious. We are currently seeing a certain shortage, though I would say it is not critical,” he said earlier this year.

“First and foremost, we have to rapidly and significantly increase production of air defence systems that are most in demand. We must also continue to improve them… Repairs at refineries must be completed more quickly.”

Amid Russian fuel shortages, Central Asian countries like Tajikistan have begun striking deals with Iran.

In August, Tajikistan’s Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency that the country is receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran. The ministry has not disclosed the route used to transport the products, but Tajikistan expects to receive 2.55 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products from Iran.

Besides Tajikistan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian welcomed a proposal from Kyrgyzstan in August to establish a joint refinery in the Central Asian country, according to a report by Iran’s Tasnim news agency

Under the agreement, Pezeshkian said, “The crude oil needed by the refinery can be supplied by Iran, and the products can be divided between the two sides.”

Will exporting oil to Central Asian countries help Iran?

The United States and Israel’s war on Iran has affected Tehran’s oil revenues. Data released by the government-administered Statistical Center of Iran in September showed that gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar.

Tehran’s ability to sell crude has also been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, imposed for most of the war, which began in late February.

Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day (bpd) in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.

TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency in September that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated that total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.

Amid these challenges, Iran has been scrambling to find new countries to trade oil with. Russian fuel shortages have opened up new opportunities for Iran in Central Asia, at least in the short term, according to analysts.

How does Iranian oil reach Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan?

Iran does not share a border with either country.

To get to Tajikistan, Iranian “oil and refined products have to cross Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan by rail”, said Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

To get to Kyrgyzstan, Iranian oil would also need to pass through Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

Is trading oil with Iran logistically sustainable for Central Asia?

“This opportunity [for Iran] depends on Ukraine continuing to hit Russian refineries, which seems unlikely, both given the waning of Ukraine’s strike capability and the US government’s demand to stop the attacks as they put too much strain on global oil markets,” he told Al Jazeera.

He noted that US President Donald Trump has pressed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly in September for an “energy truce” with Russia, since diesel prices have become a political problem for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections in the US.

“Those truces have so far collapsed within hours, but the direction is clear. Once the strikes stop, or once Russia repairs its plants, Russian fuel will come back to Central Asia duty-free under Eurasian Economic Union arrangements, and Iran will struggle to compete on price,” he said.

Logistics also favour Russia with respect to importing oil to countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, he said.

Unlike Iran, Russia shares a border with both.

“Tajikistan’s own request [for oil] would need around 51,000 rail tank cars, and its main refinery at Dangara has never operated commercially at scale. Russia, by contrast, has decades’ worth of logistics infrastructure, pipelines, rail links, and supply contracts into the region,” Schneider said.

Is Central Asia a big enough market to compensate for Iran’s Hormuz losses?

Tajikistan’s total demand, Schneider said, was about 50,000bpd.

That is a drop in the ocean compared with the 1.7 million bpd Iran exported by sea a year ago. China reported $9.96bn in two-way trade with Iran in 2025, a figure that does not include some $31.2bn in Iranian oil shipments, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.

“This suggests that Central Asia can be a useful outlet for Iranian diesel and gasoline, but it cannot replace the Chinese market,” Schneider said.

For Tehran, Central Asia’s importance depends on how the US-Israel war on Iran develops, he said, adding that Tehran also needs to stay on good terms with Russia, with which it has a deep strategic partnership.

“Iran cannot afford to be seen as poaching Russian customers too aggressively, so it will present itself as a stopgap supplier, which, again, limits how much it can earn there,” he said.

What other risks does Central Asia face in buying Iranian oil?

Schneider warned that Central Asian nations could be hit with Washington’s secondary sanctions on Iran.

“Legally, US secondary sanctions apply to any foreign company or bank that conducts a significant transaction in Iranian petroleum, wherever it is based, and the Treasury expanded the list of sanctionable conduct in August. A Treasury official has already warned publicly that anyone in this trade ‘incurs that risk themselves’,” he noted.

But Schneider said that, politically, the US sanctioning Central Asian governments is unlikely.

“Central Asia is the arena of a new ‘Great Game’ between Russia, China and the United States, and Washington is courting the region harder than at any point since the 1990s, chiefly for its critical minerals. Kazakhstan alone holds about half of the minerals the US classifies as critical, including uranium and tungsten,” he said.

“Sanctioning a Central Asian government for buying fuel from Iran would push them straight back into closer ties to Russia and China,” he noted.

“What I would expect instead are targeted designations of individual traders, rail and logistics operators and smaller banks, combined with quiet pressure on the region’s correspondent banks. That alone is enough to raise the cost and slow the trade, but will come at the price of these countries redoubling their efforts to decouple economically and financially from the US.”

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport; Saudi forces down missile near Riyadh
articles.summary: Yemeni government says one of the missiles hit Aden airport’s runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused the Houthis of firing ballistic missiles and drones at the main international airport under its control, as Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted another missile north of its capital, Riyadh.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Ministry of Transport said the Houthis targeted the runway and passenger terminal at the airport with at least two ballistic missiles and several drones.

“One of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the Yemeni flight from Cairo was to land,” it said. “We cancelled the landing of the incoming flight from Cairo [in Egypt] and diverted its route to Jeddah [in Saudi Arabia] to protect the passengers.”

The ministry also said it evacuated the airport terminal and removed two planes from the tarmac during the attacks.

It added, “This incident could easily have turned a civilian flight into a horrific humanitarian disaster, claiming the lives of dozens of innocent people in an instant.”

Aden airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control in the city that has been the seat of the government since the takeover of the capital, Sanaa, by the Iran-supported group in 2014.

The Houthis said in a statement they targeted “Saudi military supplies” arriving at the Badr camp near the airport with ballistic missiles. Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s government.

Separately, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile, launched by the Houthis, north of Riyadh.

In a social media post, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said it was tracking the launch platform used in the attack via an intelligence system over Sanaa, and promised to destroy it.

The Houthis said in statements on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday that they had targeted Saudi international airports in Riyadh and Abha.

The intensified fighting in Yemen comes amid mounting regional tensions set off by the US-Israel war on Iran. The Saudi-backed government forces launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis to retake the Red Sea port of Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Fighting has concentrated in the southwestern province of Taiz.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, described “all-out battles to take over the ground, the highlands and the mountains east of Bab al-Mandeb”.

“It’s a battle to take over the strategic western part of Taiz, and whoever controls the wider vicinity will overlook the region and have dominant military control,” he said.

“For the Yemeni government to take control of Mocha and the strategic bases and locations along the Red Sea coast, it first has to drive the Houthis off the mountains east of Mocha.”

Pakistan and Turkiye on Monday agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter Houthi attacks.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Jairam Ramesh on Wednesday criticised the Delhi Police for registering an FIR against Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Jairam Ramesh on Wednesday criticised the Delhi Police for registering an FIR against Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and other leaders over their protest against the Election Commission of India."For almost two years now the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has been relentlessly exposing, through factual evidence, the Vote Chori conspiracy hatched between the PM & the HM on one side and the CEC on the other," Ramesh said in a post on X.He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah without them, alleging that the two were “nervous, rattled and desperate” over the Opposition's campaign.“Crores of genuine voters have lost their Constitutional right to vote through the atrocious process of SIR —Shahenshah Instigated Removal. And when the LOP-LS adopts the method of satyagraha to highlight the injustices of SIR, the Delhi Police registers an FIR against him and other leaders. The diabolical duo is nervous, rattled and desperate. The writing on the wall is clear,” the post read.His remarks came after Delhi Police registered an FIR against Congress MPs Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other INDIA bloc leaders for allegedly entering the Akashvani Bhavan premises without permission during Tuesday's protest against the Election Commission.Rahul and Priyanka were briefly detained on Tuesday night following an over eight-hour sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan. The protest began after police stopped INDIA bloc MPs from marching to the Election Commission's office, located around 300 metres away, over allegations of "vote chori".According to Delhi Police, the INDIA bloc had planned to march from Parliament House to Nirvachan Sadan, the Election Commission's headquarters, without seeking or obtaining official permission.Police stopped the opposition MPs from proceeding towards the EC office, following which several leaders, including Rahul and Priyanka, staged a sit-in near Akashvani Bhavan.
