articles.title: Who says AI's killing services! An opportunity to open lakhs of new clients, jobs
articles.summary: Romal Shetty is betting that AI will give Deloitte so much more work that it will need thousands of additional employees.
articles.body: Romal Shetty is betting that AI will give Deloitte so much more work that it will need thousands of additional employees. The opportunity, he says, lies in reaching customers that the firm, one of the world's largest professional services networks, could never afford to serve before. We met the CEO of Deloitte South Asia in his Bengaluru office, overlooking the city's racecourse and one of its biggest golf courses.He's a cricket fan, and there's signed memorabilia around his office. Shetty has little time to play these days. And the conversation quickly turns from cricket to the future of consulting.Deloitte's India practice plans to add about 50,000 people by 2030, on top of the current humongous workforce of 1.5 lakh (30% of worldwide strength), of which 1 lakh serve global markets in areas like consulting, tech services, analytics, audit and tax services. That's a level of optimism you just wouldn't expect if you were looking at share prices of services and software companies over the past year.But listen to Shetty, and you might wonder: what's wrong with investors! Deloitte has traditionally worked with large corporations. Smaller businesses often assumed they could not afford it, while Deloitte questioned whether serving them would be profitable.Al changes that calculation. If machines handle most routine work, then tax advice, compliance and other services can reach smaller companies at prices they can manage. I never had this market before," Shetty says.Deloitte is piloting a platform called E-Vardhan with about 100 companies. The idea is something like an app store for business services. Customers could pick GST compliance, inventory management or working capital tools, paying a subscription instead of commissioning an expensive consulting assignment.Shetty illustrates the potential with a hypothetical Rs 10,000 monthly subscription and a target of one million small businesses. At that scale, even a modest subscription becomes a sizable business. For customers, it could mean access to expertise previously out of reach.It also changes consulting's staffing arithmetic. Instead of roughly 10 professionals serving one client, Shetty envisages one professional overseeing 10 clients, with machines doing most of the work. Even at that ratio, serving a million businesses would require 100,000 people.Five new areasThis platform approach is one of five areas Deloitte is developing. Others include increasingly autonomous services; tech products with professional support built in; helping companies improve not just their profitability but also their market value through stronger fundamentals; and investments in emerging businesses such as space and defence technology. Together, these areas account for less than 5% of revenue today. Shetty wants that to reach 45% by 2030.A lot of what's newly possible is showcased in what Deloitte calls Centre for Innovation and Technology, a 12,500 sqft space that opened two years ago, covering everything from customer experience through to factory operations. Clients can attend tailored sessions in this space, from a few hours to multi-day workshops, try out solutions, see them at work. We took a tour of it, and were reminded of the equally extensive EY.ai Centre for Reimagination that was launched in Bengaluru four months ago by EY's CEO Janet Truncale, the first such centre for the firm.Clearly, India is becoming central to global professional services companies' AI strategy.In autonomous services, Shetty points out a project to make the implementation of SAP on public cloud autonomous. Deloitte in India developed a framework of rapid configurations that cut such implementations from 6-8 months to 6-8 weeks. That gets clients running sooner and lowers their overall cost. "It's the first time anything like this has been done in the world. We had SAP's global R&D lead and Gartner analysts from Germany coming over to see it," he says.Products is another emerging space, but in association with and connected to services that Deloitte already is strong in. Shetty notes that previous attempts at products failed because implementation was left to clients.That model's changing.Aditya Kaithan, partner for technology and transformation, demonstrated an Al content generation platform that allows advertisements and marketing campaigns to be created and launched very quickly. The platform creates a brand-specific Al profile that learns preferences such as people, settings, language, tone and visual style, making content generation progressively faster. Once a campaign brief is entered, Al agents act as the copywriter, designer and brand team, developing a master brief and creative, with humans able to review and refine the direction. It can then generate and distribute content across formats such as social, email and kiosk advertising. "No shoot location, no models, no shooting team. Video is created in minutes or hours. So what was a $100,000 budget, crashes into nothing," Kaithan says.Shetty notes how suddenly all of these now become viable tor, say, a small property broker in Jaipur."We do it for top companies in the world, but we also want to do it now for small businesses," he says.Deloitte's teams in India are also building technology for global use. For a Japanese car manufacturer, they used Nvidia's Omniverse platform to simulate a factory and identify bottlenecks before construction."If they have to make 2 lakh cars a year, a car must be manufactured every 2 minutes and 32 seconds. We've been able to digitally simulate and say that these are the obstructions in, say, robotics or kinetics or physics or raw material flow that could prevent that speed of manufacturing. And then show them clearly the way out. If they had already built the factory, they would have had to spend millions of dollars to make the changesi," Shetty says. Similar solutions can be used to address, for instance, hospital flows.Across existing services, Shetty wants delivery to become at least 30% faster. But getting there requires people who understand businesses, can connect different systems and know which questions to ask. "Because you can't code without understanding the business," he says. Coding alone will not be enough.That does not mean shutting out fresh graduates. Shetty recalls two young women studying computer engineering solving an augmented and virtual reality problem in three days after an experienced team estimated weeks. Youngsters bring alterent ways of thinking, he says. Removing junior roles also risks breaking the apprenticeship through which future experts learn."If you haven't gone through the apprenticeship, how will you learn?"Shetty's own career has crossed plenty of borders. A banker's son whose family comes from Kundapur in Karnataka, he moved cities frequently while growing up. He built much of his career in telecom, including as a sector head at KPMG, and says he has worked in about 40 countries. Saudi Arabia taught him about the latest network technologies; Africa showed him how inventive companies could be with limited resources. He is now looking for that same willingness to rethink familiar problems as AI changes Deloitte's business.Enterprise technology environments are too complex. There is no way that the oroader Al technology can get into the enterprise without the services industry. People can't just go and buy an LLM and expect their problems to be solved... For IT services, there are at least two big opportunities - given their decades of experience with enterprise systems. One, they can use Al to help enterprises modernise their legacy systems substantially faster, and probably at on fifth the traditional cost. The bigger opportunity is going and having a conversation with the customer saying we're going to leverage Al to change the way you do business - look at new markets, look at new sets of customers, or completely reimagine the supply chain.As Al moves from research to real-world business applications, India's strengths become much more important. The country has decades of expertise in enterprise software, implementation and business processes. That knowledge will be critical in training and deploying the next generation of Al agents.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Madhya Pradesh: Boy Dies in Road Mishap While Fleeing After Beheading Girlfriend
articles.summary: Madhya Pradesh: 17-year-old girl allegedly beheaded by boyfriend in Rajgarh forest; suspect dies in road accident while fleeing, police recover body and saw.
articles.body: Bhopal: A 17-year-old girl was allegedly murdered and beheaded by her boyfriend in Rajgarh district in Madhya Pradesh on Sept 30, but within hours of the killing, the youth died in a road accident while fleeing the area, police said. The girl’s seven-day-old body was recovered from the forest in Biaora on Tuesday, with her skull found about 50 feet from the torso.The youth, identified as Ankit Malviya, allegedly took the girl into the forest after she travelled from Karedi to Rajgarh to meet him. Following an argument, he allegedly killed her with a saw and later called his cousin to tell him about the incident. Malviya then left the forest on his motorcycle but died after colliding with a truck, police said.Rajgarh SP Amit Tolani said the investigation had established that the two were in a relationship and that the girl had been murdered, while the youth suspected of killing her died in the road accident soon afterwards. However, the exact reason behind the killing was yet to be established.“Yes, there was a noose at the spot. We are trying to ascertain the actual reason behind the incident. The two were in a relationship,” Tolani said. Girl had been missing since Sept 30The minor lived with her maternal uncle in Karedi village and had been reported missing at Rajgarh Kotwali police station on Sept 30. Police began tracing her movements and examined CCTV footage from the area. The footage showed her travelling towards Shamsherpura on a motorcycle with Malviya, a resident of Jamonia Ganesh village.Malviya worked at a factory in Pithampur and had allegedly been in contact with the girl for around two years. Police said he had asked her to meet him on Sept 30. The girl travelled by bus from Karedi to Rajgarh, where she met Malviya. The two then travelled towards Biaora on his motorcycle.Police suspect the couple entered a forested area where an argument broke out. Malviya allegedly attacked the girl and severed her neck with a saw.After the alleged murder, police said, Malviya called his cousin and narrated what had happened. He then allegedly attempted suicide before leaving the forest.The investigation into Malviya’s call records showed that he had spoken to his cousin several times around the time of the incident. This eventually led police to question the cousin. While leaving the forest on his motorcycle, Malviya collided with a truck and died on the spot, police said.During questioning, the cousin allegedly told police about the information he had received from Malviya. Acting on the information, police searched the forest and recovered the girl’s body on Tuesday.The remains were in an advanced stage of decomposition. The skull had decomposed to a skeletal state and was found around 50 feet from the torso.A saw was recovered near the body. Police also found a rope noose hanging from a tree at the spot.While the investigation indicates that the girl was murdered and Malviya was allegedly responsible, police said the exact motive remained unclear. articles.title: New guidelines warn against obesity drugs for young children
articles.summary: Care should focus on healthy eating and exercise, not medicines such as weight-loss injections, says the World Health Organization
articles.body:
Children under 10 should not be given obesity drugs or GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, new global guidelines from the World Health Organization say.

Most of these medications are only licensed for children or adolescents older than this, but some doctors prescribe them off-label, and drug companies are testing them in children as young as six.

WHO says the care should focus on healthy eating and exercise, not medicine or surgery, although they do not oppose drug trials.

Some digital technology, such as activity trackers and any online games that encourage the player to be more active and move, might be useful, it says, based on the limited evidence available.

Estimates suggest 170 million children and adolescents worldwide are obese.

That includes 70 million children aged 5–9. Obesity prevalence in this age group has quadrupled since 1990, rising from 2% to 8%.

In 2024, 35 million children under the age of five were overweight.

Obesity increases the risk of many different diseases, including type 2 diabetes.

Dr Luz De Rigil, Director of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO, said: "For children under 10, WHO does not recommend obesity medicines, bariatric surgery or weight-management devices. This is a strong recommendation."

These might be appropriate for older children and adolescents when lifestyle approaches have failed and if the individual is "mentally and physically prepared" for the treatment, she added.

She said WHO recognises this is an evolving field and will continue to evaluate the evidence.

WHO's head of Nutrition and Food Safety Actions, Laurence Grummer-Strawn, said: "We are particularly concerned in this age group, if you are starting children very early on to using a GLP-1 or drugs like this, when does that stop?

"We don't really have evidence that you can use this as a temporary treatment and then turn to something dietary later on in life.

"We are very cautious about jumping in without clear evidence," he said.

articles.title: Delhi HC seeks Centre's response on body cameras on cops during protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has asked the Centre to consider a PIL seeking mandatory use of body-worn cameras by police during protests and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has asked the Centre to consider a PIL seeking mandatory use of body-worn cameras by police during protests and crowd-control operations, saying the issue should not be treated as a “grey area” requiring court intervention.The court asked the Centre to take a decision on the plea within six months.A bench headed by Acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambhre said any direction on the use of body-worn cameras would have wider implications for policing and could not be confined to the Delhi Police alone.The bench observed while hearing the plea, “Why should we direct them to legislate? It cannot be said that it is a grey area.”The court questioned the need for judicial intervention when existing laws already provide for regulation of police procedures in areas covered by the legislature.The PIL, filed by Chahat Raghav, seeks directions for the mandatory use of body-worn cameras by Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel deployed during protests and crowd-control operations. It also seeks a comprehensive framework governing the storage, retention, integrity and evidentiary use of footage recorded by the cameras.The petitioner has cited the use of body-worn cameras by traffic police and a tender issued for their procurement, arguing that the technology is already available to the authorities.Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that body-worn cameras could enhance transparency and accountability during protests, especially in cases involving allegations of police excesses and counter-allegations against protesters.Sibal said the cameras were already being used by police in some situations, but only sporadically. He argued that the Delhi Police's 2022 standing order on rallies and demonstrations did not specifically provide for body-worn cameras and that a clear protocol was needed.He also disputed that the existing videography mechanism was sufficient, saying the recording under the standing order was different from footage captured by cameras worn directly by police personnel involved in crowd control.Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the respondents, submitted that the Delhi High Court's PIL rules require a petitioner to first approach the concerned authorities through a representation. He said the present petition could be treated as such a representation.Sharma also submitted that the Supreme Court, while hearing a matter concerning protests at Jantar Mantar, had directed the authorities to frame an SOP and that the existing mechanism already provides for videography of protests. The court recorded the ASG's statement and directed the respondents to communicate their decision on framing an SOP for the use of body-worn cameras within six months.The petitioner was given liberty to approach the High Court again in case of any inaction.The move comes amid heightened security in the New Delhi, Central Delhi and North Delhi districts following a series of demonstrations against the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.Police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed in large numbers, with multilayered barricades placed at several points to prevent protesters from entering restricted areas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Psychology says children who hide small problems until they become big ones may be learning something unexpected
articles.summary: A child comes home upset because a friend ignored them. They lose a small amount of money at school but say nothing.
articles.body: A child comes home upset because a friend ignored them. They lose a small amount of money at school but say nothing. They make a mistake in class, get a warning from a teacher or have a problem with a friend and still keep quiet. Then, days later, the problem becomes much bigger and the parents finally find out. It is easy to ask, “Why didn't you tell me earlier?” But children do not always stay silent because they do not trust their parents. Sometimes, they are learning from what happens after they speak.Children may start deciding which problems are worth sharingAs children grow, they become more aware that not every part of their life needs to be reported to a parent. Research on adolescent disclosure has found that young people make different decisions about what they tell parents depending on the type of issue. A study of 118 early and middle adolescents found that nondisclosure could have different reasons. Some young people avoided telling parents because they expected disapproval, while others considered an issue personal or not serious enough to discuss. This means a child who keeps a small problem to themselves may be thinking, “I can handle this,” “It isn't important enough,” or “I don't want this to become a big discussion.” That decision can sometimes backfire when the problem continues or grows.The reaction may teach the child whether to speak next timeOne of the clearest findings comes from a longitudinal study of 982 young people. Researchers looked at how parents' positive and negative reactions to disclosure were connected with later secrecy and openness. They found that negative reactions were associated with young people feeling more controlled and less connected to their parents. Those feelings, in turn, were linked with increased secrecy and reduced disclosure. Positive reactions were associated with greater connection and more disclosure.This does not mean parents should never correct a child. A parent may need to set a boundary, explain consequences or intervene when something is unsafe. The important part is what happens before the correction. If a child says, “I had a fight with my friend,” and the first response is “What did you do?” followed by a long lecture, the child may remember that experience the next time something happens. They may decide it is easier to stay quiet.A child may also be trying to solve the problem aloneKeeping something private is not automatically unhealthy. Research on adolescent-parent disclosure shows that young people do not see every area of their lives as something parents are entitled to know. In a study of 276 adolescents, participants disclosed more to mothers than fathers, particularly about personal matters. Greater trust and parental acceptance were associated with more disclosure and less secrecy. So a child who does not immediately mention a small friendship problem may simply be trying to work it out independently. The concern comes when this becomes a pattern: the child repeatedly hides problems, waits until the situation is serious, or becomes visibly worried about what will happen if a parent finds out.What parents can do when the child finally tells themThe first conversation after a child finally opens up can influence whether they speak earlier next time. Instead of starting with, “Why didn't you tell me?”, try: “I'm glad you told me now. Tell me what happened.” Then ask: “Do you want me to listen, or do you want help fixing it?” If the problem is small, resist the urge to immediately take control. Give the child a chance to explain what they have already tried. Parents can also make it clear that telling them about a problem does not automatically mean losing control over the situation. Research on parental monitoring has similarly found that adolescents' negative reactions to monitoring were associated with less disclosure, suggesting that a parent's approach to getting information can affect how willing a young person is to share.The goal is not to make children report everythingChildren do not need to tell parents every disagreement, embarrassing moment or minor mistake. What matters is whether they believe they can tell a parent when something becomes difficult. A child who says, “I didn't tell you because I thought I could fix it myself” is very different from one who says, “I didn't tell you because I knew you would get angry.” The first may be developing independence. The second may be learning that silence feels safer than speaking. And that is the unexpected lesson behind many delayed disclosures: sometimes, the size of the problem is not what determines whether a child talks. What they expect to happen after they talk can matter just as much.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘We’re short of resources’: France’s student protesters, in their own words
articles.summary: French students and teachers protesting school conditions spoke with Al Jazeera about their demands.
articles.body:
Paris, France – At least 250,000 students, teachers and parents protested across France on Tuesday , supported by trade unions and rights groups.

The demonstrations have grown since students began blockading the entrances to their high schools on September 17, starting in the Paris suburb of Creteil. The movement quickly spread throughout the city’s suburbs, with high schoolers protesting against conditions, lamenting dilapidated buildings, shortages of teachers and staff and overcrowded classrooms.

The blockades were met by a muscular police response, with riot police sent to break up the student protests.

More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, 85 percent of them aged under 18. At least 10 investigations into police misconduct have been opened by France’s police watchdog IGPN.

On October 2, France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray met with student leaders and the government announced a five-point plan to reform the public education system – an olive branch students agreed was insufficient to address the crisis.

Some 210 teenagers – including one who lost a hand – and 715 police officers have been wounded, according to officials.

Anne Savinel-Barras, president of Amnesty International France, called on authorities to “avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force”.

“Footage and testimonies widely reported over the last week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and restraint techniques by police. Tear gas grenades have been discharged recklessly, and rubber bullets have been fired causing serious injuries.”

Al Jazeera spoke to several protesters about their demands:

‘Macron’s government has to stop investing only in war’

Theo, 19, student : “This is my first demonstration. I’m here in solidarity with the high schoolers, after this week of blockades and police oppression. I’m also here for other demands: for universities, for more resources for schools, and not just schools but hospitals too. We’re really short of resources.

“Macron’s government has to stop investing only in war. We’re fed up. That’s why we’re all here together in this movement of solidarity, young and old. We all have the same demands: a better future.”

‘Teachers are absent, and compared with schools in Paris we don’t have the same resources’

Olympe, 16, high school student : “We blockaded our school all week to demand our rights and to denounce what’s happening in our schools. Teachers are absent, and compared with schools in Paris we don’t have the same resources. We’re given less money, and we don’t have the same privileges.”

Rania, 15, high school student: “We don’t feel listened to at all. We feel inferior, especially considering that we’re the future. So when no one listens to us, we do all this, but in the end will it really change anything? We don’t know.”

Maissene, student : “We came to support our classmates, simply because if they’re blockading, we blockade too. It’s a general movement, and they can’t do it on their own.”

Raphael, 17, high school student : “We came to defend our youth. Because we’re young, the state doesn’t listen to us. They think we have no political awareness and don’t know what we’re defending. We’re here to show the opposite: we know exactly what we’re defending. We know our values.”

Rose, 16, high school student: “If nothing changes, we’ll keep going for much longer. On October 17, there will be a big demonstration, with high schoolers, students and farmers. So it’ll be a bit like a new revolution.”

‘More resources, more teachers, better teaching conditions’

Clemence, 30, maths teacher in Paris : “I support the high schoolers’ movement 100%. Their demands are ones we’ve been making for years. Today, we’re taking the opportunity to march alongside them. They’re asking for more resources, more teachers, better teaching conditions. We’ve been asking for this for years, because the state badly neglects it … You saw how the heatwave was handled: our classrooms were between 35 and 40°C. It’s unacceptable.”

Clara, 20, fashion student: “I’m here first of all in support of the high schoolers who started this strike in the 93 [Seine-Saint-Denis]. It’s where I live, and I know these schools. They have always lived and worked in unacceptable conditions. Their demands are legitimate, and they have a right to be heard and listened to.

“So far I think the atmosphere is rather good. You can see everyone is mobilised, proud and happy to be here. But you can also feel a lot of anger, because for once we want our demands to be heard, and we want people to listen to this youth that has been complaining for several years.”

‘We were peaceful, and they chose violence’

Tina, a 20-year-old student: “Yesterday we had a general assembly at our university, and the police and riot police were called in by our own administration. We said that was unacceptable. They started blocking our university, blocking our ideals of defending the high schoolers and the current cause. We don’t find that normal, so we came to demonstrate with them today to show our support. In the end there were no classes. We hadn’t finished expressing ourselves. We were peaceful, and they chose violence.”

articles.title: Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason
articles.summary: Former German spy chief August Hanning was detained on Tuesday on suspicion of attempted treason ‌in a case that ranks among Germany’s biggest intelligence scandals since the Cold War.
articles.body: BERLIN — Former German spy chief August Hanning was detained on Tuesday on suspicion of attempted treason ‌in a case that ranks among Germany’s biggest intelligence scandals since the Cold War. Prosecutors accused him of paying for secret documents and using them in an analysis for a foreign spy service. They did not identify the intelligence service and it was not immediately clear whether the analysis reached its intended recipient. The arrest of a former head ​of Germany’s foreign intelligence is unprecedented and could damage the country’s intelligence relationships with allied nations, according to a senior security lawmaker. “Hanning is ​strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason and espionage,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement. The ⁠Spiegel news magazine reported late on Tuesday that investigators were pursuing a possible connection to Azerbaijan. It reported Hanning had been in contact with ​an agent from the country. The federal prosecutor’s office declined to comment on the report. Hanning did not respond to a request for comment. The chancellery ​declined to comment. Five years after his seven-year tenure as head of the BND foreign intelligence service ended in 2005, Hanning agreed with a former BND office manager to receive confidential intelligence information in exchange for payment, according to prosecutors. The office manager, identified as Manfred D. in line with privacy rules, was also arrested on Tuesday, and both were ​due to appear before a judge at the Federal Court of Justice. Manfred D. served as office manager to successive BND presidents until March 2026, ​potentially giving him access to some of Germany’s most current intelligence at the time that prosecutors say documents were being siphoned from the service. ‘No compromises’ Prosecutors said D. is ‌suspected of ⁠having supplied around 2,000 documents over the years, including classified material intended solely for internal use within the BND and senior-level intelligence briefings at the chancellery. Those included documents relating to the Iranian nuclear programme and the Russian military, as well as highly sensitive material classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries, Sueddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) newspaper reported. Prosecutors said Hanning had used classified information supplied by D. to prepare an analysis for an officer of a ​foreign intelligence service and for years shared ​political information with a representative ⁠of the spy agency. The case does not involve Russia, according to information obtained by Sueddeutsche Zeitung. Conservative security expert Roderich Kiesewetter told the Handelsblatt newspaper on Tuesday that the case could strain relations with Germany’s intelligence allies, saying espionage ​cases of this kind were “particularly burdensome for trust and particularly damaging for Germany”. BND President Martin Jaeger said the ​agency had launched ⁠extensive internal investigations as soon as suspicions emerged, adding, “There can be no compromises on internal security.” Past spy scandals Hanning’s arrest is the latest in a series of notorious espionage scandals in Germany. West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign in 1974 after it was revealed that an East German spy had worked as ⁠his close aide ​for nearly two years. In 1990, senior West German counter-intelligence official Klaus Kuron was ​exposed as a Stasi spy and later convicted of treason. More recently, former domestic intelligence chief Hans-Georg Maassen said in 2024 he was being monitored by the security agency he once ran ​over alleged right-wing political extremism, which he denied.
